blocks.title: How to read this chapter
paras: This chapter is orientation, not science. It explains how the Handbook grades evidence and where its limits are. The science starts in [[exercise-science|Exercise science]].

blocks.text: Fitness does not lack information. The information is unsorted. A careful review of many trials and a confident video reach you through the same feed, in the same format, with the same air of authority. Nothing tells you which claim rests on twenty trials and which rests on an explanation someone found plausible.

The result is rarely that people fail to train. They train for years while changing what they do, and never build enough uninterrupted progress in one direction to see a result. What is usually missing is not effort. It is a stable framework, and a way to tell strong claims from weak ones.
This Handbook aims to tell you what to do, and also how confident anyone should be that it works.
It is a reference covering training, nutrition, recovery, physique and tracking progress. Your Levlofit plan tells you what to do today. The Handbook explains why.

blocks.text: Two rules follow. An explanation of how something might work inside the body is not a result, and does not justify a recommendation by itself. And "not established" means the question is open, not that the answer is no.

blocks.title: A useful habit
paras: When you meet a confident fitness claim, do not ask only whether it is true. Ask what someone would have had to measure to know it. Many popular claims fail that question straight away.

blocks.text: These are working defaults, not scientific findings.

items: **Consistency beats intensity.** The plan you follow for two years beats the better plan you follow for six weeks.
**Technique defines the load.** A repetition done differently is a different exercise, whatever the log says.
**Recovery is part of training.** It is an input to adaptation, not a reward for having trained.
**Progress is measured in months.** Change from week to week is mostly noise: water, sleep, food timing and measuring error.
**Evidence first, then what you will keep doing.** Where the evidence is absent, choose the option you will actually sustain.

blocks.text: One number makes a poor target. Body weight cannot separate muscle gained from food eaten, and a mirror cannot separate real change from better lighting. Track several things, because they move at different speeds and rarely all stall at once.

blocks.text: Training works because a signal, repeated often enough and recovered from well enough, changes your muscle. Exercise choice, sets, rest, food and sleep all exist to protect or strengthen that signal.
This chapter explains the signal and the few variables that control it. Read it once, then come back whenever a later recommendation seems arbitrary.

Adaptation is a change in your body that makes a hard demand easier. Lift a load your body is not yet equipped for, recover, and you become a little better equipped. Stop the demand and the change slowly reverses. That is also why a plan you have outgrown stops working even though nothing about it changed.

head: Adaptation
What changes
Roughly how fast
rows: Better coordination and confidence under load. The muscle is not bigger yet.

blocks.text: These timescales are a teaching guide, not measured limits for you. The order still matters. Early strength gains come quickly and often before your body visibly changes, so do not expect the mirror to keep up with the bar in the first weeks.

The leading explanation for muscle growth is **mechanical tension**: the force a muscle fibre experiences as it works against resistance. Fibres that are recruited and work hard receive the signal to build.
The practical point is this: judge a set by whether its last repetitions were truly hard with acceptable technique. A set stopped far short of that is likely to do less.

blocks.title: In practice
paras: "Feeling the muscle" and "getting a pump" are sensations. They do not tell you by themselves that a set will build muscle.

blocks.text: A common story says training damages muscle and the body repairs it bigger. The measurements do not support it as the main cause.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: In ten young men followed through ten weeks of training, muscle damage and protein synthesis were both highest in the first week, but neither was related to muscle growth. By weeks three and ten, damage had fallen and the rise in protein synthesis correlated strongly with growth (r about 0.9). This is one small study of mechanisms. {damas2016}

blocks.text: The authors conclude that growth comes from many small rises in protein synthesis, as damage fades. Two things follow in practice:

items: **Soreness is not a score.** A new exercise or a long break can leave you very sore. A well-run session months later can leave you less sore and still be useful.
**Do not chase damage.** Seeking soreness adds recovery cost, and that cost can come out of your next session.

blocks.text: Once tension is the signal, planning comes down to three questions: how much hard work, how often, and how hard.
Volume means hard working sets per muscle per week. It has the clearest link to growth.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong for more volume, moderate for the shape of the curve
paras: The American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) position stand found that growth was enhanced by 10 or more sets per muscle group per week, with a dose-response. {acsm2026}

A review of 67 studies found that size and strength both rise with volume, with diminishing returns that are much stronger for strength. Counting an assisting set as half a set predicted results best. {pelland2025}

blocks.text: So more tends to give more, and each extra set buys less. The Handbook gives no personal target above 10 sets, because your recovery, history and stress decide what you can use. Count a set that trains a muscle directly as one, and a set where it assists as half. Rows train your biceps. Presses train your triceps.

With weekly volume equal, training a muscle more often did not change growth. It does appear to help strength: the ACSM found strength was enhanced by 2 or more sessions a week, and could not determine an upper limit. {acsm2026} {pelland2025}
In practice, frequency is mainly a way to deliver volume. Spreading many sets across more days can keep the later sets from fading.
**Repetitions in reserve (RIR)** is how many more repetitions you could have done with acceptable technique when you stopped. Two left is 2 RIR. No more possible is 0 RIR, called momentary failure.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate that hard training is enough; insufficient that failure adds anything
paras: A review of 15 studies found no advantage for growth from training to momentary failure over stopping short (effect size 0.12, confidence interval -0.13 to 0.37). A looser definition of failure gave a trivial advantage (0.19, 0.00 to 0.37). The authors suggest a possible non-linear relationship. {refalo2023}
A later analysis found growth improved as sets ended closer to failure, while strength barely changed. Its authors call it exploratory, because the RIR values were estimated. {robinson2024}
The ACSM reports that training to momentary fatigue did not consistently affect outcomes, and its main recommendation is to train with high effort. {acsm2026}

blocks.text: These fit together if benefit grows as a set becomes truly hard, then flattens before failure. That is a hypothesis, not a proven curve.

head: Goal
Reasonable default
Why
rows: A practical default. Growth may suffer if you stop far short, and failure has not been shown to add more.
Strength looks similar across a wide range.
Not shown to be necessary for either.

blocks.text: Shorter rest makes training feel harder. That does not make it more productive.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate for a small benefit past about a minute; insufficient that short rest harms growth
paras: A review of 9 studies found intervals crossing zero at every site: arm 0.13 (-0.27 to 0.51), thigh 0.17 (-0.13 to 0.43), whole body -0.08 (-0.45 to 0.29). The authors read this as a small benefit from resting more than 60 seconds, and no clear further gain past 90 seconds. Six of the studies used untrained people, and they ran for only 5 to 10 weeks. {schoenfeld2024}
The ACSM found no strength difference between rest under and over one minute, and not enough data to say whether rest length affects growth. {acsm2026}
An earlier review concluded that the research does not support needing shorter rest for growth than for strength. {henselmans2014}

blocks.text: Rest until the next set is limited by the target muscle, not by your breathing. Heavy compound lifts usually need longer to perform well. Cutting rest is a fair way to fit a session into less time. Treat it as a time choice, not as progress.
A hard session leaves a signal and leaves fatigue. How you feel in the next day or two mostly reflects the fatigue, so that is a poor time to judge your plan.

Older books draw a neat "supercompensation" curve with a perfect window for your next session. Train, recover and come back stronger is sound. A window you can time is **not established**. Use what you can observe instead: session performance, joint comfort, sleep, appetite and motivation. [[recovery|Recovery]] covers these.
Your body adapts to what you actually do. Heavy, low-repetition work builds the skill of lifting heavy. Plenty of hard work in a moderate range builds more size. These overlap but are not identical.
It also applies to movements. You mostly get better at the exercise you practise, so keep exercises long enough to progress on them.

People respond differently to the same training. Genes play a part. So do sleep, food, stress, history and skill, and those you can influence. Averages tell you where to start, not where you will end up. Your own log, over months, becomes the better guide.

Most of this comes from studies lasting weeks to months, mostly in young adults, often men. The direction is fairly consistent. The precision is not, which is why you will see ranges rather than exact numbers.

blocks.title: See a clinician
paras: This chapter describes normal training in healthy adults. Persistent pain, unexplained loss of strength, or symptoms that do not settle with rest are not things to adjust in your training. See a qualified clinician.

title: Learning a lift
summary: The six movement patterns, how to learn a new exercise, and when to add weight.

blocks.text: Good technique means repeating the same movement, under control, through a range you own. Learn each lift light, and add weight only when every rep looks and feels the same.

blocks.title: Levlofit rules
paras: These are Levlofit coaching rules, not research findings; technique coaching is hard to test in trials. A qualified coach can check your form in person.

items: **Start light.** Bodyweight, a light dumbbell or an empty bar.
**Same setup.** Place your feet, hands and grip the same way on every rep.
**Control the way down.** Lower the weight under control instead of dropping into the bottom.
**Use the range you own.** Go as deep as you can while keeping your position, without pain.
**Check it.** Film one set from the side and compare it with the exercise demo.
**Then add weight.** Only when every rep looks the same, keeping 2 to 3 reps in reserve while you learn.

blocks.text: A warm-up has one well-supported benefit: a better session. Other benefits are claimed on much weaker grounds. This chapter separates them and gives you a warm-up short enough that you will keep doing it.
Mobility is here because the two get confused. A warm-up prepares you for today. Mobility work changes your range over months.
The aim is to get ready, not tired.

head: What it does
How
rows: Practising the exact lift with gradually heavier loads.
Rising loads show how today is going before a hard set.

blocks.title: Evidence: emerging
paras: A review of passive heating, such as baths, saunas and heated clothing, found warmer muscle develops force faster. Maximal voluntary force did not rise. A warmer muscle gets to a force sooner. It does not become stronger. This review did not study active warm-ups, which do much more than raise temperature. {rodrigues2022}

head: Claimed benefit
Grade
What is supported
rows: Dynamic stretching improves jumping and sprinting compared with no warm-up. This is the benefit to rely on. {li2023}
Warmer muscle produces force faster, without raising maximal force. {rodrigues2022}
A single session of static stretching reduces stiffness. {ingram2025}
A real benefit that research has not settled. Use it if it helps.
Do not treat this as your reason to warm up. See below.

blocks.title: Injury risk
paras: "Warm up so you do not get injured" is the most repeated reason, and not a secure one. Do not count on a warm-up or stretching to protect you.

The stronger evidence points to strength training itself. Across six randomised trials with 7,738 people aged 12 to 40, it cut sports injury risk by about two thirds (relative risk 0.338, 0.238 to 0.480), and more training was linked with more protection. Most of those people were athletes, so applying this to gym training is a reasonable step, not a tested one. {lauersen2018}

blocks.text: **Dynamic stretching** moves a joint through its range under control, such as leg swings, arm circles, bodyweight squats and walking lunges. **Static stretching** holds a stretched position still.

head: Approach
Effect on jumping and sprinting
rows: Improved jump height and sprint time. The steady choice.
Ranked highest for jump height, and clearly better than no warm-up.
Ranked lowest for jump height, and made sprint time worse.
No significant difference from no warm-up.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: This comes from a network analysis of 35 studies, with dynamic stretching for 7 to 10 minutes showing the largest effect. Most studies were not randomised and few used blinding, so treat the ranking as a guide. {li2023}
Hold length matters too. Static stretching of 60 seconds or more per muscle cut performance by 4.6%, against 1.1% for under 60 seconds. {behm2016}

items: If a stretch lets you reach a position you otherwise cannot, use it, keep it short, then do dynamic movement and warm-up sets.
If you have no such limit, dynamic work alone is enough and faster.
Avoid long static holds as your only preparation right before heavy or explosive work.

blocks.text: These studies measured jumping and sprinting, which may react more than an ordinary set of 8 to 12 repetitions.

Time
Purpose

blocks.text: These times are practical guides. **Warm-up sets matter most**, and they are the stage people skip. They rehearse the exact movement, and they tell you something: when a normal load feels heavy today, you find out before committing to a hard set. If you are short of time, cut the general stage, not these.

blocks.title: On activation drills
paras: Glute bridges before squats and band work before pressing are popular and cheap. It is **not established** that they add anything beyond warm-up sets. Keep them if they help you. Drop them before you drop your warm-up sets.

blocks.text: Later exercises in a session need only one or two light sets.
Mobility is the range you can actively reach and control. Range you can only be pushed into is not much use under load.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A review of 65 studies found stretching does not lengthen muscle: fascicle length did not change after one session or many. Stiffness fell after both. Tolerance to the stretch rose only after repeated stretching. {ingram2025}
Regular stretching builds range, and in one review its volume, intensity and frequency did not play a significant role in how much. {konrad2024}
Strength training through a full range gave range of motion gains similar to stretching. {afonso2021}

items: **Train mobility separately.** A warm-up uses the range you have. New range takes weeks to months.
**Pick a method you will keep up.** Regular practice matters. Exact hold times matter less than people claim.
**Lift through your full range.** It builds usable range while you train anyway.
**Target the real limit.** A muscle can feel tight without being what limits you. Test one position, work on it, and retest weeks later.

blocks.title: Stretching into pain
paras: Mild discomfort is expected. Sharp, radiating or joint-line pain is not. Stop, and see a qualified clinician rather than stretching harder.

head: Session
Focus
Typical movements
rows: Arm circles, band pull-aparts, upper back rotations, push-up variations
Shoulder blade drills, dead hangs, light rows
Bodyweight squats, walking lunges, leg swings, ankle rocks

items: **Skipping warm-up sets to save time.** Your first hard set becomes the warm-up.
**Long static holds as your only preparation.** Follow them with dynamic work. {li2023}
**Warming up until tired.** Getting breathless uses energy your working sets need.
**Treating foam rolling as a performance boost.** Use it if it makes a position more comfortable.
**Expecting a warm-up to fix a mobility limit.** That takes months.
**Relying on the warm-up for injury protection.** The evidence points to strength training. {lauersen2018}
The demonstrated benefit of warming up is a better session.
Warmer muscle produces force faster, not more maximal force.
Dynamic work helps. Long static holds alone just before explosive work do not.
Warm-up sets matter most and double as a recovery check. Activation drills are optional.
Stretching does not lengthen muscle. Range improves through lower stiffness and more tolerance.
Protection from injury is better supported for strength training than for warming up.

title: Progressive overload
summary: The one variable that separates training from exercising.

sources.pelland2025: Pelland JC et al. The resistance training dose response: meta-regressions exploring the effects of weekly volume and frequency on muscle hypertrophy and strength gains. Sports Med 2025;56(2):481-505. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w

blocks.text: A muscle adapts to the demand it faces. Once it has, that same demand only maintains it. **Progressive overload** means raising the demand often enough that adapting stays necessary.
This chapter is about the bookkeeping: raising the demand over months without collecting more fatigue or risk than the gains are worth. Most of it is practical guidance, labelled as such.

"Add weight to the bar" is one method. For a beginner it is usually the best one, but it is not the real requirement. The requirement is that **the hard, well-performed work a muscle does should trend up over time**.
An extra repetition, an extra hard set, or the same work through a fuller range all count. You will need them eventually, because load cannot climb forever.

blocks.title: In practice
paras: If you cannot say what improved since last week, perhaps nothing did. Log your sets. Without a log, training drifts into repeating work you have already adapted to.

head: Variable
What it does
When to use it
rows: Raises the demand of each repetition directly.
First choice for beginners and big lifts with small weight steps.
More work at the same load. Bridges big jumps in weight.
When the next weight step is too big to take cleanly.
Raises weekly volume, which has a clear link to growth, but costs the most recovery and time. {pelland2025}
Over months, when load and repetitions slow and you have recovery to spare.
Early, then always. Treat full range as the standard.
Recovers what a too-easy set left behind. Failure has not been shown to add more. {refalo2023} {acsm2026}
When sets are stopped well short of hard. It runs out quickly.
Puts the load on the muscle you mean to train.
Always. Everything else depends on it.

blocks.text: These are not a menu to rotate for variety. Over the long term: technique and range first, then load and repetitions together, then volume, then effort as a controlled adjustment.

blocks.title: Cutting rest
paras: Shorter rest makes a session feel much harder, which is why it gets mistaken for progress. With less rest you usually do less work on the next set, and recording that as improvement is a bookkeeping error.

It is also not proven to cost you muscle. A review of 9 studies found intervals crossing zero, with a small benefit past 60 seconds and no clear gain past 90. The ACSM found not enough data on rest and growth. So cutting rest is not progress, and short rest does not ruin your results. {schoenfeld2024} {acsm2026}
Log it as fitting the session into less time.

blocks.text: Three more things look like progress and are not:

items: **Adding exercises.** A longer session is not a harder one for each muscle. Exercises that repeat a pattern add fatigue and time.
**Changing the plan.** Something new brings soreness and a fresh feeling, and it resets your numbers, so real progress becomes impossible to see.
**Adding load by shortening range.** A heavier partial repetition is a different, easier exercise with the same name.

blocks.text: **Double progression** is the default here because it prevents a very common mistake: adding load before you own the current one.

items: Give each exercise a repetition range, not a fixed number.
Keep the load the same and add repetitions until every working set reaches the top of the range with good technique.
Only then add load. Your repetitions fall back toward the bottom of the range, and the cycle repeats.

blocks.text: Technique sets the top of the range. A repetition with a changed movement path does not count.
Here is an example: a range of 8 to 10, three sets, on incline dumbbell press with dumbbells rising in 2.5 kg steps.

head: Week
Load
Repetitions per set
Decision
rows: Keep the load. Not every set is at the top.
Range complete. Add load next session.

blocks.text: Week 5 is where people give up. Repetitions falling after a load increase is the method working. Other approaches work too, but this one needs no percentages, no maximum tests, and no maths beyond reading your own log.

Take the smallest load increase available. A 5 kg jump on a heavy squat is a small percentage. The same 5 kg on a lateral raise is huge, which is why small-muscle exercises often stall. When the jump is too big:

items: Add repetitions until you are comfortably past the top of your range, then jump.
Add the new load to one set at a time over several sessions.
Use small fractional plates on barbell lifts if your gym has them.

blocks.text: Slowing down is normal. Beginners may add load almost every session. Later, progress can take months. Reading a normal slowdown as a broken plan often leads you to break it. Check the cheap explanations first:

head: Check
What a problem looks like
rows: Short or broken sleep in the weeks before the stall.
Body weight flat or falling while you are trying to gain muscle.
Sessions missed or cut short. Count what you completed, not what you planned.
Sets ending several repetitions short of hard while logged as hard.
Several exercises falling at once, with poor sleep, low motivation or joint aches.

blocks.text: A stall on one exercise is an exercise problem. A stall on most exercises at once points to recovery, and more work is the wrong answer. [[plateaus|Plateaus]] covers true stalls.

items: **Adding load by calendar instead of performance.** Technique slips to absorb it, and your log records progress your muscle never saw.
**Treating every session as a test.** Most sessions should be repeatable, not maximal.
**Changing exercises before progressing on them.** Progress needs a stable reference.
**Expecting every exercise to climb together.** Big lifts and small ones do not move at the same pace.
**Logging what you meant to do.** Record what happened, including bad sets. A log of only good days cannot show a stall.
Hard, well-performed work must trend up. Load is one way, not the definition.
Cutting rest, adding exercises, changing plans and shortening range are not progress.
Double progression: fill the repetition range, then add load.
Use the smallest step available. The percentage jump is what matters.
Check sleep, food, consistency and effort before deciding a plan has failed.

title: Recovery
summary: Training creates the signal. Recovery decides what happens to it.

sources.craven2022: Craven J et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytical review. Sports Med 2022;52(11):2669-2690. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y
sources.dobrosielski2021: Dobrosielski DA et al. The association between poor sleep and the incidence of sport and physical training-related injuries in adult athletic populations: a systematic review. Sports Med 2021;51(4):777-793. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01416-3

blocks.text: Rest is one input to recovery. Recovery is the outcome: fatigue clears, and the signal from training turns into adaptation.
This chapter covers what has real evidence, says where the evidence is thinner than the fitness industry suggests, and gives you signals you can actually watch.

A hard session creates a signal to adapt, and it creates fatigue. What you feel in the next day or two is mostly the fatigue. Recovery depends on sleep, on eating enough, and on not stacking another big demand too soon.
Without a real training signal, sleep and protein have nothing to act on. Recovery decides how much of the signal is carried out.
Sleep has clear evidence behind it for training performance, and it is often the first thing people trade away.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A review of 69 publications found sleep loss lowered exercise performance by about 7.6% on average, across every category tested. Performance fell about 0.4% for each extra hour awake before exercise. The effects were consistent for going without sleep or waking earlier than normal, and less consistent for going to bed late. Results varied widely between studies and 89% of participants were men, so the size for any one person is uncertain. {craven2022}

blocks.text: One finding helps with planning: afternoon and evening sessions after a poor night consistently suffered, while morning sessions were largely unaffected. If a bad night is unavoidable, train earlier if you can. {craven2022}

blocks.title: Evidence: insufficient on sleep and injury
paras: You will often hear that poor sleep raises injury risk. A review of 12 cohort studies concluded that current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for injury in adult athletes, while noting the studies were too mixed to settle the question. {dobrosielski2021}

blocks.text: This is no argument for sleeping less. The case for sleep rests on performance, which has good support.
These are practical habits, not findings from the papers above.

items: Keep your wake time steady, including at weekends.
Give yourself enough time in bed. You control that directly.
Keep your room dark and cool.
If late caffeine or alcohol affects your sleep, move or drop it.

blocks.text: Recovery has a material cost. **Energy** decides whether your body has resources to build. Gaining muscle while eating well below your needs is possible in some situations and harder in others. **Protein** supplies what repair and building use. [[protein|Protein]] gives the amounts and Indian sources.
The biggest recovery lever you control is how much you asked for in training.

head: Lever
Effect on recovery demand
rows: The main driver. More volume brings more signal and more cost.
Failure adds fatigue, and has not been shown to give consistently better results. {acsm2026}
In practice, heavy compound lifts tire you more per set than machine isolation work.
The same weekly sets over more days can keep later sets from fading.

blocks.text: **Rest days** are part of the plan. They need not be still: walking and ordinary activity are fine. They do need to be easier than a training day. A "light" day that becomes a hard session is an unlogged training day.

Exams, work and personal pressure can reduce how much training you can handle, even if your plan has not changed. In practice, let volume move with your life. Cutting sets during a hard month and restoring them later keeps you consistent. Holding volume and missing sessions does not.

No home device directly measures recovery. Treat sleep scores and readiness numbers as weak inputs, and do not let them overrule your logged performance. These practical signals are cheaper and more useful:

head: Signal
Recovering well
Under-recovered
rows: Load or repetitions rising over weeks, with an occasional flat day
Several unrelated exercises falling for over a week
Quiet, or briefly stiff then fine
Aches that outlast sessions and build week to week
Falling asleep normally, waking fairly rested
Trouble falling asleep, or waking early despite being tired
Both low for several days with no other reason

blocks.text: One bad session is noise. A week of them across several exercises, plus two or more other rows, is worth acting on. See [[deload-week|Deload week]].

items: **Soreness is not a recovery reading.** It often reflects unfamiliar work.

**Recovery tools are not recovery.** Do not expect massage guns or similar tools to replace sleep and food. Regular cold-water immersion had a harmful effect on strength gains from resistance training in one review (effect size -0.60, -0.87 to -0.33), so avoid making it a habit if strength is your goal. {malta2021}
**Total inactivity is not required.** Light movement is fine.
**Supplements do not replace the basics.** They do not make up for too little sleep or food.

blocks.title: Beyond a training adjustment
paras: Ordinary fatigue responds to less training. These do not. See a qualified clinician:
Sharp, localised or lasting pain, especially at rest or at night.
Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern.
Fatigue, unexplained weight loss or falling performance that continues after several weeks of truly reduced training.
Missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain alongside low food intake. These may point to low energy availability, which is a medical concern.
Distress about food, weight or missed sessions that affects daily life.
This Handbook does not diagnose and does not replace individual care.

items: Recovery turns a training signal into adaptation.
Sleep loss lowers performance, more so for afternoon and evening sessions.
It is not established that poor sleep alone raises injury risk.
Your biggest recovery lever is how much you asked for in training.
Soreness and readiness scores are weak signals. Logged performance across exercises is stronger.
Lasting pain, nerve symptoms or fatigue that survives real rest are medical questions.

title: Building a push session
summary: How to build a pressing day from principles, not a list.

blocks.text: A push session trains the muscles that press weight away from you: chest, front and side shoulders, and triceps. They work together, which makes the grouping convenient. Nothing requires you to train them this way.
Your Levlofit plan builds your sessions for you. This chapter teaches the reasoning, so you can judge a session, swap an exercise sensibly, or build one for your own equipment.
Think of a session as an ordered set of slots, each with a job. Two arguments support this, resting on different evidence.

**Order.** The ACSM found strength was better when an exercise was trained at the beginning of a session rather than the end. Exercise order did not affect muscle growth. So put what you most want to get stronger at first. {acsm2026}
**Coverage.** Different exercises can grow different parts of a muscle.

blocks.title: Evidence: emerging
paras: In 30 trained people who trained each leg differently for 8 weeks, leg extensions favoured one part of the quadriceps and leg press favoured another. This is one lower-body study. Applying it to pressing muscles is reasoning, not a tested result. {burke2025}

head: Slot
Job
rows: The heaviest, most technical press, done first.
Another pressing angle, or a more supported press, adding work at lower technical cost.
A single-joint movement for the chest.
Lateral raises, because pressing gives side shoulders little direct work.
Direct work, after presses have already tired them.

blocks.text: This is a checklist for coverage, not a law.
Choosing an exercise for a slot
A slot names a job, not an exercise. Apply these in order:

items: **Equipment.** Start with what you actually have.
**Joints and injury history.** Remove anything that irritates a known problem.
**Skill.** If you have less experience, prefer a shorter learning curve for the same job.
**Fatigue.** Free weights ask more of your stabilising muscles. That is easiest to afford early. Later, a machine often lets you keep working the target muscle for less overall fatigue.

blocks.title: Evidence: insufficient on free weights and machines for growth
paras: The ACSM found strength was not affected by free weights versus machines, and not enough data to say about growth. It also concludes that many forms of resistance training work. {acsm2026}

blocks.text: So choose the version you can load progressively and do consistently.
Two exercises can replace each other when both are the same movement pattern and load the same joint action.

A flat barbell bench press and an incline dumbbell press are both presses using the shoulder and elbow in the same way. A cable fly is not a substitute for either. It targets the same muscle, but the elbow stays largely fixed, so it belongs in the isolation slot.
Use this test on any exercise, including ones this Handbook does not name.

**Volume** is hard sets per muscle per week, with assisting sets counted as half. Every press also counts as triceps work. The ACSM found growth was enhanced by 10 or more sets per muscle group per week, and a separate review found diminishing returns as sets rise. Reach about 10 if you can, then adjust based on recovery. {acsm2026} {pelland2025}

**Effort** is how close you get to failure. Make the final repetitions truly hard. Failure is not required, and it has not been shown to give consistently better results. [[exercise-science|Exercise science]] sets out the evidence. {refalo2023} {robinson2024} {acsm2026}

**Frequency** is how often you train a muscle. For strength, the ACSM found 2 or more sessions a week helped, and could not determine an upper limit. With volume equal, frequency did not change growth. {acsm2026} {pelland2025}
There is **no established fixed recovery time** such as 48 hours. It varies with the person, the exercise and the work done. Use the signals in [[recovery|Recovery]].
These dials add up. Raising volume without thinking about effort and frequency is a common route to a plan you cannot recover from.

Nothing supports shorter rest as better. A small benefit appears past about 60 seconds, with no clear further gain past 90. The ACSM found no strength difference, and not enough data on growth. {schoenfeld2024} {acsm2026}
Rest until the target muscle, not your breathing, limits the next set. Heavy presses usually need longer than isolation work to perform well.

head: Model
How it works
Best for
rows: Fill a repetition range at one load, then add load.
Most muscle-building work. Repetitions absorb good and bad days.
Add load at a fixed, usually low, repetition target.
Strength work. The ACSM links loads of 80% of your one-repetition maximum or more with greater strength gains. {acsm2026}
Change load or sets based on how today's sets went.
Weeks where your recovery varies a lot.

blocks.text: Match the model to your goal and repetition range. Load affects strength, but growth was not affected by loads from 30% to 100% of your maximum in the ACSM review. Heavier is not required for size. {acsm2026}

[[warmup-mobility|Warm-up and mobility]] covers the evidence. For a push session: a few minutes of light activity, shoulder and upper back movement, then gradually heavier warm-up sets of your main press. Warm-up sets matter most. If time is short, cut the general part.
Plan recovery by which muscles you trained and how hard, not by session names. A chest day and a shoulder day share shoulder and triceps work whatever they are called.
This is one complete example, not a prescription. It fills the slots above so you can check your own reasoning.

Count it per muscle: chest gets 10 direct sets, side shoulders get 6, and triceps get 6 direct sets plus half of the 7 press sets, about 9.5. Chest reaches 10 in this one session. Rest figures are ranges because the evidence does not support exact numbers.

items: **Skipping warm-up sets.** Your first working set becomes the warm-up.
**Swinging on isolation work.** It moves the load off the muscle you meant to train.
**Going past your repetition range.** A load that undercuts the range throws away the reason you chose it.
**Shortening range to add load.** See [[progressive-overload|Progressive overload]].
**Changing exercises so often no method gets a fair trial.** Progress needs a stable reference.
**Treating shorter rest as progress.** It is a time choice.
A push session is a set of slots with jobs, not a fixed list.
Put what you most want to get stronger at first.
Aim for about 10 hard sets per muscle per week. Returns shrink as you add more.
Train hard. Failure is not required.
Nothing supports shorter rest as better.
Choose exercises for fatigue and ease of learning. Machines and free weights both work.

title: Building a pull session
summary: How to build a pulling day from principles, not a list.

sources.acsm2026: Currier BS et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Resistance training prescription for muscle function, hypertrophy, and physical performance in healthy adults: an overview of reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
