blocks.text: A pull session trains the muscles that draw weight toward you: lats, middle and upper back, rear shoulders, biceps and forearms.

Back training is often sold as a fix for desk posture. It is **not established** that strengthening your back changes your usual posture, or that doing so would bring a health or performance benefit. Train your back because it is a large part of your muscle, because balanced development is a fair goal, and because pulling strength is worth having.

A pull session uses slots too, for the same reasons as [[push-sessions|Building a push session]]: order helps strength, and different exercises may develop different parts of a muscle. {acsm2026} {burke2025}

Include both vertical pulling (pulldowns, pull-ups) and horizontal pulling (rows), because they load your back along different lines. "Pulldowns for width, rows for thickness" is gym shorthand that no study measured. Do both for coverage.

head: Slot
Job
rows: The heaviest, most technical pull, done first.
The pattern the main pull did not use.
A machine or cable movement through a full range.
Direct work, because pulling gives it limited work.
Direct arm work, once your back is no longer the limit.

blocks.text: The same four tests apply: equipment, joints, skill and fatigue. Three points are specific to pulling:

items: A pull-up or barbell row asks more skill and grip than a machine row or pulldown. With less experience or energy, the supported option is a fair choice.
**Grip can end the set first.** If your hands give out before your back, your back has not done the work you intended. Straps, a different grip or a machine all solve this.
The main slot is where a hard, technical movement is cheapest, because you are freshest.

blocks.text: A wide-grip pulldown and a pull-up can replace each other. Both are vertical pulls with the same joint actions, though the pull-up asks more stability. A seated cable row cannot replace either. It is a horizontal pull, so it belongs in the second slot.
The evidence in [[push-sessions|Building a push session]] applies unchanged.

One point matters more here: **biceps get work from every pulling set**. Counted as half a set each, heavy rows and pulldowns already give your biceps real volume before your first curl. Counting indirect sets this way predicted results best in one large review. {pelland2025}
If your arms are stalling or always sore, look at your total pulling sets before you add curls.

The three models from the push chapter apply. Pulling adds one wrinkle: bodyweight moves go up in big steps. You cannot add a small amount to a pull-up as you can on a pulldown, so add repetitions first and only add weight when your range is full. Assisted versions allow finer steps.
Use the same three parts, aimed at your shoulders, upper back and grip. Warm-up sets matter most.

A pull session shares recovery with anything that loads your biceps, forearms or the back of your body, including heavy Romanian deadlifts on leg day. Plan by the muscles you actually trained, using the signals in [[recovery|Recovery]], not a fixed number of hours.
This is one example, not a prescription.

Your upper arm stays behind your body on an incline curl, which loads the biceps at a longer length. Partial repetitions at long muscle lengths gave more growth than those at short lengths in one review, though that does not directly test this exercise. {strey2026}
Six direct biceps sets look modest until you count the nine pulling sets at half each. That makes about 10.5 biceps sets from this session.

items: **Swinging.** It moves the load onto your lower back and hips.
**Pulling with your arms.** Start the movement from your shoulder blades.
**Using more load than your grip can hold.** The set ends before your back has worked.
**Skipping rear shoulder work.** It needs its own slot.
**Adding curls to fix stalled arms.** Check your total pulling sets first.
**Using one pattern for both pull slots.** Two rows or two pulldowns cover only one line of pull.
Cover both vertical and horizontal pulling.
Back training does not need a posture claim to justify it.
Every pulling set also trains your biceps. Count it as half.
Grip limits are real. Solve them instead of pushing through.
Recovery follows the muscles you trained, not the name of the session.

title: Building a leg session
summary: How to build a leg day from principles, not a list.

sources.burke2025: Burke R et al. Exercise selection differentially influences lower body regional muscle development. J Sci Sport Exerc 2025;7:449-459. doi:10.1007/s42978-024-00299-4
sources.acsm2026: Currier BS et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Resistance training prescription for muscle function, hypertrophy, and physical performance in healthy adults: an overview of reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
sources.strey2026: Strey B et al. Muscle hypertrophy from partial repetition at long vs. short muscle length: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sport Sci Health 2026;22:33. doi:10.1007/s11332-025-01586-5

blocks.text: A leg session trains your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calves. These include some of your largest muscles, and their big lifts are among the hardest most people do, so order matters a lot.

Go from the heaviest, most technical lift down to single-joint work that handles fatigue well. Include a squat pattern and a hip hinge, because they load the front and back of your leg in different ways.

blocks.title: Evidence: emerging
paras: Thirty trained people did different exercises with each leg, twice a week for 8 weeks. Leg extension favoured the rectus femoris, part of the quadriceps. Leg press favoured the vastus lateralis, another part. Straight-leg calf raises favoured one calf muscle, the medial gastrocnemius, with no clear result for the lateral gastrocnemius or soleus. This is a single study. {burke2025}

blocks.text: So big lifts may not make isolation work unnecessary, and the reverse may be true too.

head: Slot
Job
rows: The heaviest, most technical lift, done first.
Hamstrings and glutes, which the squat pattern does not fully cover.
Usually a machine, adding quad work at lower technical cost.
A straight-leg raise, a bent-knee raise, or both if you have the equipment.

blocks.text: Filling two slots with squat patterns and skipping the hinge trains the front of your leg twice and neglects the back.

The four tests from [[push-sessions|Building a push session]] apply. Joints matter especially here: a barbell squat loads your spine in a way a leg press or hack squat does not, so a lower-back problem can be reason enough to choose the supported option.

A barbell back squat and a hack squat can replace each other. Both are squat patterns using your knees and hips. A leg press cannot replace a Romanian deadlift: one is a squat pattern and the other a hinge. Swapping them leaves the hinge slot empty.
Range of motion and partial repetitions

Full range is the default. The ACSM found strength improved with a complete range of motion, though it found not enough data on range and growth. Load gained by shortening your range is not progress. {acsm2026}
"Partial repetitions are always wrong" goes too far, though.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate for long over short; insufficient for partials over full range
paras: In a review of 8 studies, training at longer muscle lengths, the stretched part of a movement, gave more growth than training at shorter lengths (effect size 0.283, 0.04 to 0.52). The advantage was clear at the far and central parts of the muscle. {strey2026}
The review compared these two partial ranges with each other. It does not show that partials beat a full range.

items: Train through a full range by default.
A partial done on purpose in the stretched position is a fair tool, such as when a joint limits the other part of the range.
A partial done because the load is too heavy is still a mistake. Decide before the set, not after.
A quarter squat cuts out the stretched part, which is the part this evidence favours.

blocks.text: The evidence in [[push-sessions|Building a push session]] applies. No fixed recovery time for legs, such as 72 hours, is established.

In practice, heavy squats and hinges are demanding, and many people handle them less often than pressing or pulling. Test that against your own log. The claim that calves recover fast enough to train daily is **not established**. Train them as often as you can sustain and progress.
The three models from the push chapter apply. Adjusting by feel can suit squats and hinges, since it may catch a tired day before your technique breaks down.

For strength, the ACSM links loads of 80% of your one-repetition maximum or more with greater gains. For growth, load from 30% to 100% made no difference, which is how a leg extension can build quadriceps despite a modest number on the stack. {acsm2026}

Use the same three parts, aimed at your hips and ankles. Warm-up sets matter most here, where your main lift is heaviest. Tight ankles can limit squat depth. It is **not established** that warming them up changes your results, so test whether your own depth improves, and keep the work if it does.
A leg session's demand often makes it the session to plan around. Remember that a heavy hinge shares work with pulling sessions through your lower back and grip.
This is one example, not a prescription.

Leg press and leg extension are both here on purpose, because they favoured different parts of the quadriceps. {burke2025} The seated curl keeps your hip bent, which holds your hamstrings at a longer length.

items: **Cutting depth to add load.** A quarter squat is a different, easier exercise.
**Skipping the hinge.** This is a common gap in leg sessions.
**Assuming big lifts make isolation useless.** Early evidence points the other way.
**Bouncing out of the bottom of a squat.** Stay in control where the load on your muscles is greatest.
**Scheduling by a fixed clock.** Use your log.
**Skipping calves because progress is slow.** Slow is not the same as absent.
Cover both squat and hip-hinge patterns.
Big lifts and isolation work may develop different parts of a muscle.
Put your main lift first.
Full range is the default. A deliberate partial in the stretched position is defensible. One caused by too much load is not.
No fixed recovery time is established for legs. Check your own log.
Load drives strength. For size, hard sets matter more than the number on the bar.

title: Changing push exercises
summary: When to change an exercise, and when not to.

sources.acsm2026: Currier BS et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Resistance training prescription for muscle function, hypertrophy, and physical performance in healthy adults: an overview of reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
sources.burke2025: Burke R et al. Exercise selection differentially influences lower body regional muscle development. J Sci Sport Exerc 2025;7:449-459. doi:10.1007/s42978-024-00299-4
sources.strey2026: Strey B et al. Muscle hypertrophy from partial repetition at long vs. short muscle length: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sport Sci Health 2026;22:33. doi:10.1007/s11332-025-01586-5

blocks.text: Variation is a tool for specific problems, not something your plan needs on a schedule. This chapter covers when changing an exercise is worth it, what it costs, and what a second good selection looks like.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: The ACSM found periodised programmes were not significantly better than non-periodised ones for healthy adults, given good progressive overload, and concluded periodisation is less important than once thought. It found not enough data to say whether varied exercise selection affects growth, and concluded that many forms of resistance training work. {acsm2026}

blocks.text: So if variation is not needed, changing an exercise should have a real reason. "It has been a while" is not one.

Two other popular reasons are also weak. It is **not established** that repeating a movement harms your joints when technique and recovery are sound, or that variation protects them. Feeling fresher is a real reason, as a preference. A plan you will follow beats a slightly better one you abandon.

Progress needs a stable reference. An exercise changed every few weeks cannot show improvement, because there is no unbroken run of numbers. A new movement also takes practice, so at first your coordination may limit you before your muscle does.
If you are still progressing on an exercise, keep it.

head: Reason
Grade
What to do
rows: Swap to a movement in the same slot that does not cause the symptom. See a clinician if pain continues.
Apply the swap test and move on.
A different exercise may develop a different part of the muscle. {burke2025}
First rule out the causes in [[progressive-overload|Progressive overload]].
Fair. Change something, note it, and accept that your numbers reset.
Not a demonstrated mechanism, and not a reason.

blocks.text: The slots from [[push-sessions|Building a push session]] do not change. Only the exercise in each slot does, chosen with the same four tests. Volume, effort, frequency, progression and warm-up all stay.

items: **Main press:** flat barbell bench instead of incline dumbbell press. Same pattern and joint action. The barbell takes away the balance demand of two separate weights and lets you lift more. It is a different trade, not a better exercise.
**Second press:** incline machine press instead of flat machine press. Same pattern and slot, at a different angle.
**Isolation slots:** pec deck, machine lateral raise, single-arm cable lateral raise, EZ-bar extension and single-arm pushdown each match their counterparts in target and joint action.

blocks.text: An overhead triceps extension loads part of your triceps at a longer length than a pushdown does. Evidence for long lengths comes from comparing partial ranges, mostly in legs, so treat this as a reason to include one, not as proof. {strey2026}
This is one example, not a prescription. It fills the same slots with different choices.
This is a second good selection, not an upgrade. Running the first example for a year and never touching this one is a fair choice.

items: **Changing on a schedule.** It costs your reference numbers and buys nothing the evidence can identify.
**Expecting full strength on a new exercise.** Lower loads at first are normal, not a step back.
**Changing more than one thing at once.** A new exercise and new volume in one week gives a result you cannot explain.
**Hiding a lift you dislike behind "variation".** Dropping it may be right. Just name the real reason.
**Using variety instead of overload.** Something new is not the same as something harder.
Variation is not required. Periodised plans were not found better for healthy adults.
Changing costs you your reference numbers and some practice time. Keep what is still working.
Good reasons: joint irritation, equipment, coverage, a true stall, or honest motivation.
Slots, volume, effort, frequency, progression and warm-up stay the same when an exercise changes.
A second good selection is an alternative, not an upgrade.

title: Changing pull exercises
summary: When to change a pulling exercise, and when not to.

sources.acsm2026: Currier BS et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Resistance training prescription for muscle function, hypertrophy, and physical performance in healthy adults: an overview of reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
sources.burke2025: Burke R et al. Exercise selection differentially influences lower body regional muscle development. J Sci Sport Exerc 2025;7:449-459. doi:10.1007/s42978-024-00299-4
sources.strey2026: Strey B et al. Muscle hypertrophy from partial repetition at long vs. short muscle length: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sport Sci Health 2026;22:33. doi:10.1007/s11332-025-01586-5
sources.pelland2025: Pelland JC et al. The resistance training dose response: meta-regressions exploring the effects of weekly volume and frequency on muscle hypertrophy and strength gains. Sports Med 2025;56(2):481-505. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w

blocks.text: [[push-variation|Changing push exercises]] sets out the position: variation is not required. {acsm2026} This chapter gives a second good way to fill the pull slots, and says when that is worth the cost.

items: **Grip and forearms.** If your hands limit the set before your back does, move to machine-supported pulling or use straps.
**Coverage.** Different lines of pull work your back differently, and different exercises may develop different parts of a muscle. The direct evidence is from legs, so this is reasoning. {burke2025}
**Bodyweight limits.** A pull-up goes up in big steps and may be out of reach at first. A pulldown adjusts finely in both directions. Switching is a loading decision.

blocks.text: Without one of these or another good reason, keep what you are still progressing on.
The slots from [[pull-sessions|Building a pull session]] stay. Volume, effort, frequency, progression and warm-up do not change with your exercise choice.

items: **Main pull:** wide-grip lat pulldown instead of a pull-up. Same vertical pattern and joint action, less stability demand and much finer loading steps.
**Second pull:** seated cable row instead of chest-supported row. Same horizontal pattern. Your free torso adds light trunk work, but also makes it easier to swing.
**Other slots:** single-arm dumbbell row, reverse pec deck, EZ-bar curl and cable curl each work in their slots.

blocks.text: A cable curl with your elbow behind your body, or an incline curl, loads your biceps at a longer length than a standing EZ-bar curl. The evidence favouring longer lengths compared partial ranges and is indirect here. {strey2026}
This is one example, not a prescription.
As before, six direct sets understate your biceps work. The ten pulling sets add about five more when counted at half each. {pelland2025}

items: **Changing on a schedule.** It costs your reference numbers and buys nothing the evidence can identify.
**Swinging your body.** A free-torso row makes this easy. It shifts work to your hips and lower back.
**Pulling with your arms.** Your arms already get indirect work.
**Shortening your range to add load.** On pulls, this usually loses the stretch, the part worth keeping.
**Losing rear shoulder work when you change exercises.** Check that the slot is still filled.
**Adding load before you have learned a new variation.** Coordination comes first.
Variation is optional. Change for grip, coverage, loading steps, a true stall or honest motivation.
Machine pulling lets you work your back hard with less grip fatigue. It is a real trade, not a lesser option.
Rear shoulder work is the slot most easily lost. Check for it.
When you shorten a pull, the stretch is usually what goes. Protect it.

title: Changing leg exercises
summary: When to change a leg exercise, and what single-leg work does.

sources.acsm2026: Currier BS et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Resistance training prescription for muscle function, hypertrophy, and physical performance in healthy adults: an overview of reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
sources.burke2025: Burke R et al. Exercise selection differentially influences lower body regional muscle development. J Sci Sport Exerc 2025;7:449-459. doi:10.1007/s42978-024-00299-4
sources.kassiano2025: Kassiano W et al. Comparison of muscle growth and dynamic strength adaptations induced by unilateral and bilateral resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2025;55:923-936. doi:10.1007/s40279-024-02169-z

blocks.text: Variation is not required, as [[push-variation|Changing push exercises]] explains. {acsm2026} This chapter gives a second good way to fill the leg slots, and covers single-leg training.

items: **Spine loading.** A barbell back squat loads your spine in a way a hack squat or leg press does not. A lower-back limit is a concrete reason to change your main lift.
**Coverage.** Different exercises developed different parts of the quadriceps in a study of exactly these muscles. {burke2025}
**Equipment.** Leg training depends heavily on what your gym has.

blocks.text: Without a reason, keep the exercise you are still progressing on.
Split squats, lunges, single-leg presses and single-leg hinges are often sold as better than two-leg work. The evidence is more specific.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate for strength being specific; insufficient for a difference in growth
paras: A review of 9 studies found you get stronger at the version you train. Two-leg training gave more two-leg strength (effect size 0.56, 0.16 to 0.96), and single-leg training gave more single-leg strength (-0.65, -0.93 to -0.37). {kassiano2025}

For muscle growth it found no significant difference (-0.21, -3.56 to 3.13). That interval is very wide, so this does not show the two are equal. It shows the research cannot yet tell. The authors call the literature limited. {kassiano2025}

blocks.text: Training one side at a time does show what each side can do. That follows from how it is done. It is **not established** that this corrects a difference between your sides better than two-leg work does.
Small side-to-side differences are common. Marked, lasting or painful ones are a reason to see a clinician, not to add more single-leg sets.
Good reasons to use single-leg work are practical: limited equipment, a spine-loading limit, preference, and seeing each side in your log.

A swap must match the movement pattern. A Bulgarian split squat is a knee-driven squat pattern on one leg. It cannot fill the hinge slot, because that leaves your hinge undone. For a single-leg hinge, use a single-leg Romanian deadlift.

items: **Main squat:** hack squat instead of barbell back squat. Same pattern, more support, and less load on your spine.
**Hip hinge:** single-leg Romanian deadlift instead of the two-leg version. Same pattern. You trade total load for balance and a view of each side.
**Second quad lift:** keep this multi-joint. Replacing it with a second isolation exercise may lose what it adds. {burke2025}
**Isolation slots:** a lying leg curl and seated calf raise replace the seated curl and standing raise, changing the length at which those muscles work.

blocks.text: Volume, effort, frequency and rest do not change with your exercise choice. No fixed recovery time is established. A set on each leg is one set per leg, not two sets. Counting it as two inflates your log without adding work to either side.
This is one example, not a prescription.
The hinge slot uses an actual hinge, and the second quad slot stays multi-joint. With no hack squat, a Bulgarian split squat is a reasonable choice in the main squat slot, at a lower load.

items: **Swapping across patterns.** A squat pattern does not fill a hinge slot.
**Counting a per-leg set as two.** It inflates your log.
**Replacing multi-joint work with more isolation.** They may add different things.
**Cutting depth on single-leg work to add load.** Balance will limit your load first. That is expected.
**Changing on a schedule.** It costs your reference numbers.
**Chasing perfect symmetry.** Small differences are common.
Variation is optional. Change for spine loading, coverage, equipment, a true stall or honest motivation.
A swap must match the pattern. A split squat is not a hinge.
Single-leg and two-leg work show no established difference in growth. Strength is specific to what you train.
Single-leg work shows each side. That it corrects differences is not established.
Keep the second quad lift multi-joint.

title: Deload week
summary: Reducing training stress, and how little we actually know about it.

sources.bell2023: Bell L et al. Integrating deloading into strength and physique sports training programmes: an international Delphi consensus approach. Sports Med Open 2023;9:87. doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00633-0

blocks.text: A deload is a planned or chosen period of less training stress. The idea is near-universal among coaches: build up fatigue, pull back, return fresher. It is also under-researched, and this chapter keeps what is reasoned, what coaches agree on and what has been measured apart.

blocks.title: Evidence: insufficient that deloading is required
paras: An international panel of strength and physique coaches calls deloading "ubiquitous yet under-researched", and says how to fit it into training for the best results is unknown. The authors also say it is unclear whether deloading is a necessary part of training to avoid the harmful effects of overtraining. What follows is expert opinion and practical experience, not trial results. {bell2023}

blocks.text: The panel's definition: "a period of reduced training stress designed to mitigate physiological and psychological fatigue, promote recovery, and enhance preparedness for subsequent training." {bell2023}

So you keep training, with less stress. Its purpose is to prepare you for what comes next. It does not build anything by itself. It is also different from a **taper**, which peaks you for a competition.

head: Claim
Grade
Comment
rows: Coaches widely report it. Controlled trials are lacking. {bell2023}

blocks.text: That makes deloading **low cost and low certainty**. It is reasonable to adopt, as long as nobody claims more for it.

The paper's background reports that deloads are generally done every 4 to 6 weeks for about 7 days, ranging from one session to two weeks. That describes common practice, not a trial result. {bell2023} So this Handbook sets no required schedule.
Coaches on the panel agreed a deload could be planned in advance or decided by how you feel. {bell2023} The default here is the second: reduce when your own signals say so. Watch for a pattern:

items: Performance falling across several unrelated exercises for more than a week.
Normal warm-up loads feeling heavy.
Joint aches that outlast sessions and build week to week.
Trouble falling asleep, or waking early despite being tired.
Appetite and motivation both low for several days with no other reason.

blocks.text: One of these is noise. Several together, lasting, are a reason to reduce. If you prefer a planned lighter week, that is also fine.

The clearest point in that paper is universal agreement that **training volume should come down**, through fewer sets or repetitions. On intensity, the coaches accepted more than one approach: it could stay the same or drop. {bell2023}
So reduce volume first. Lowering the weight while keeping every set is unlikely to be the best version.

head: What
Normal week
Lighter week
rows: Clearly fewer. This is the main lever.
Same or lower. Pick one, so you can read the next week.
Unchanged. A lighter week is a poor time for new movements.
Usually unchanged, which keeps the habit. Fewer days also works.
Normal. Eating less works against the purpose.

blocks.text: Here is an example of a pressing session:

head: Exercise
Normal week
Lighter week
rows: 2 sets, well short of hard, 65 kg

blocks.text: Sixteen hard sets become about eight comfortable ones. Nothing should feel difficult. If the week leaves you as tired as normal, you did not reduce enough.
A full break is right when you are ill, injured, or dealing with something that needs the time. [[recovery|Recovery]] lists the symptoms that need a clinician instead of a training change.
Otherwise, reducing is usually the better choice, for a practical reason: the session you still turn up for is easier to continue from than the one you skipped.

items: **Turning a lighter week into a normal one.** If every set still ends hard, volume came down only on paper.
**Lowering weight but keeping every set.** Reduce sets first.
**Testing yourself.** A personal record attempt defeats the purpose.
**Eating less.** Recovery has a cost.
**Using it to rescue a plan you cannot recover from.** If you need a lighter week very often, your usual volume may be too high.
A deload means less training stress, not stopping.
It is under-researched, and whether it is necessary is unresolved.
No required schedule is established. Let your signals guide you, or plan one if you prefer.
Coaches agree that volume should come down. They accept different approaches to intensity.
It is low cost and low certainty. Reasonable to adopt, unreasonable to insist on.

title: Breaking through plateaus
summary: Telling a real plateau from normal slowing.

sources.craven2022: Craven J et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytical review. Sports Med 2022;52(11):2669-2690. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y
sources.acsm2026: Currier BS et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Resistance training prescription for muscle function, hypertrophy, and physical performance in healthy adults: an overview of reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897
sources.pelland2025: Pelland JC et al. The resistance training dose response: meta-regressions exploring the effects of weekly volume and frequency on muscle hypertrophy and strength gains. Sports Med 2025;56(2):481-505. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w
sources.refalo2023: Refalo MC et al. Influence of resistance training proximity-to-failure on skeletal muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med 2023;53:649-665. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01784-y

blocks.text: Most things called plateaus are not. Progress naturally slows as you train for longer, and it can look like a problem because your first months set an expectation that was never going to last.
Normal slowing needs patience. A true stall needs a diagnosis, and the answer is rarely the plan itself.

head: What you see
What it usually is
rows: Noise from sleep, food, stress or timing. Do not act on it.
Same load on one exercise for a few weeks, repetitions rising
Slower than six months ago, still rising
One exercise flat for several weeks, others rising
An exercise problem. You can diagnose it.
Most exercises flat or falling at once
A recovery problem. See [[recovery|Recovery]] and [[deload-week|Deload week]].

blocks.title: The key difference
paras: A stall on one lift and a stall on most lifts are different problems. Treating them the same is why people add work when they should cut back.

blocks.text: You need a log to tell them apart. Without one, ordinary ups and downs look like a trend.
Start with the checks in [[progressive-overload|Progressive overload]]: sleep, food, consistency, effort and fatigue. Three deserve extra attention:

items: **Effort.** Sets logged as hard that were not can cause a stall your log will not show.
**Food.** Body weight flat or falling while you are trying to gain muscle explains many stalls blamed on the plan.
**Sleep.** Sleep loss lowers performance, more so in afternoon and evening sessions. If your sleep was short in the weeks before a stall, take it seriously. {craven2022}

blocks.text: These causes are practical, not ranked by research. Work through them in this order:

head: Cause
What to do
rows: The next weight step is too big
Common on small-muscle exercises. Add repetitions, or use smaller plates.
Load rose because the movement got smaller. Go back to full range at a lower load.
Grip on pulls, lower back on hinges, triceps on presses.
Film a set and compare it with an older one.
The exercise does not suit you
The last resort. Swap with the test in [[push-variation|Changing push exercises]], and accept that your numbers reset.

blocks.text: Falling performance across several unrelated lifts points to recovery. **Adding work is the wrong answer.** Reduce volume first, then re-check after a week or two.
If that does not restore progress within a few weeks, look outside the gym: food, sleep, stress or health. See a clinician about lasting pain, nerve symptoms, or fatigue that survives real rest.
Once you have a diagnosis, the useful levers are the ones you already know. No special plateau technique is needed.

items: **More weekly sets,** if you have recovery to spare. Volume has the clearest link with growth, with returns that shrink. It is also the most expensive lever. {acsm2026} {pelland2025}
**Truly hard sets,** if you were stopping well short. Going all the way to failure has not been shown to add more. {refalo2023} {acsm2026}
**Full range,** if your range had shrunk.
**More frequent sessions,** mainly as a way to fit in your sets. {pelland2025}
**Time.** Nobody wants this one, but progress is meant to slow.

blocks.title: Changing your whole plan is a weak fix
paras: The instinct is to replace the plan. The ACSM found periodised programmes were not significantly better than non-periodised ones, and that many forms of training work. A new plan can feel like progress through novelty and soreness while resetting the numbers that would show if anything improved. {acsm2026}

blocks.text: You will also see terms like minimum effective volume and maximum recoverable volume, presented as measurable numbers. They are useful as words for an idea: too little does little, and too much cannot be recovered from. It is **not established** that anyone can measure them for you, so this Handbook gives no numbers for them.

items: **Acting on one bad session.** Wait for a pattern.
**Changing several things at once.** You will not know what worked.
**Adding work when performance is falling everywhere.** It makes things worse.
**Adding load at the cost of technique or range.** Your log shows progress that did not happen.
**Judging the plan on one stalled lift.** Isolation exercises stall often and say little about the rest.
**Comparing your pace with someone else's.** Your history and circumstances differ.
Most plateaus are normal slowing.
One stalled exercise and many stalled exercises need opposite responses.
Rule out sleep, food, consistency and effort first.
If everything is falling, reduce. Do not add.
Replacing your whole plan is a weak fix, and it resets your numbers.

title: Injury prevention
summary: What protects you, and what only sounds as if it does.

sources.lauersen2018: Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med 2018;52(24):1557. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099078

blocks.text: Nearly every gym habit gets defended on injury grounds, and many of those defences are untested. This chapter starts with the finding that has real evidence behind it.
The best-supported protection is training itself

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: Across six randomised trials with 7,738 people aged 12 to 40 and 177 injuries, strength training cut sports injury risk (relative risk 0.338, 0.238 to 0.480). Strength of evidence was rated high. A 10% rise in training volume cut injury risk by more than four percentage points. {lauersen2018}
Limits: the review covered sports injuries in athletic groups. It shows regular strength training is protective in those groups. It does not tell you how often a given gym exercise hurts people.

blocks.text: So the most supported protection is the training itself, progressed sensibly and kept up for years. Anything that keeps you training consistently helps. Anything that keeps interrupting training has a cost, including too much caution.

head: Claim
Grade
Comment
rows: More training was linked with more protection. {lauersen2018}
Warm up because it improves your session.
Do not rely on it for protection.
Fits the evidence above. Not tested alone here.
Hard to test and widely accepted.
Machines are safer than free weights
They differ in joint demand and stability, which affects your choice. That is not a safety ranking.

blocks.text: Most of what you control is here. It is practical guidance, not proven by a trial, but a sensible reason still counts for something.

items: **Take the smallest step available.** The percentage jump is what matters.
**Do not raise load and volume in the same week.** If something starts hurting, you will not know why.
**Treat a return from a break as a return.** Do not restart at the loads you left at.
**Be patient with tendons.** It is commonly explained that tendons adapt more slowly than muscle. No practical timeline is established, so treat this as a reason for patience, not a schedule.
**Cut back when several exercises fall together.** See [[recovery|Recovery]] and [[deload-week|Deload week]].

blocks.text: Good technique is widely accepted and hard to test directly. It stays a default because the reasoning is sound and following it costs nothing.

items: **Load gained by shortening your range is not progress.** See [[leg-sessions|Building a leg session]] for when a partial is fair.
**Stop a set when your technique changes.** This is more useful than hitting a repetition number, and it avoids the open question of how close to failure to go.

blocks.text: Hard training is uncomfortable. Discomfort and pain are different things, and it is worth learning the difference early.

head: Expected
Stop and get it checked
rows: Sharp, stabbing or localised joint pain
Pain that worsens with each repetition
Soreness in the next days, especially after new work
Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you at night
Swelling, a joint giving way, or lost movement
Mild stiffness that eases as you warm up
Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern

blocks.text: Anything in the right column means stop that exercise and find the cause. Training through it can turn a manageable problem into a long one.

blocks.title: Beyond a training adjustment
paras: This Handbook does not diagnose. See a qualified clinician for:
Pain that is sharp, localised, present at rest, or wakes you at night.
Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern.
Swelling, a joint giving way, or sudden loss of range.
Any pain that has not improved after two weeks of truly reduced loading.
Fatigue or falling performance that continues after several weeks of reduced training.
Missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain alongside low food intake. These may point to low energy availability, a medical concern.
Distress about food, weight or missed sessions that affects daily life.
Getting checked early is not too cautious. It helps protect the consistency that matters most.

items: Did I do warm-up sets on my first heavy exercise?
Did those warm-up loads feel normal today?
Did I keep full range on every working set?
Did I stop each set when my technique changed?
Did I change only one thing this week?
Does anything match the right column above?
The best-supported protection is strength training itself, progressed sensibly and kept up.
Warm up for performance. Do not count on it to prevent injury.
It is not settled that stretching prevents injury.
Load management and technique are sensible defaults, not measured effects.
Learn the difference between discomfort and pain. The right column means stop.

title: Nutrition fundamentals
summary: The few things that decide most of the outcome.

sources.aragon2017: Aragon AA et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets and body composition. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:16. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0174-y
sources.issnprotein: Jager R et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:20. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8
sources.whocarb2023: World Health Organization. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. Geneva: WHO, 2023.

blocks.text: Nutrition advice can make hundreds of decisions look equally important. They are not. A few things account for most of your result, and the rest only becomes worth your attention once those are handled.
This chapter sets out that order and the words the rest of this volume uses.
This order is practical guidance, built on the sources cited below.

head: Priority
What
Why it sits here
rows: Decides whether your weight goes up or down. Nothing below this overrides it. {aragon2017}
Helps decide how much of a weight change is muscle. {issnprotein}
A diet you abandon delivers nothing. Long-term success depends on it. {aragon2017}
Food quality, fibre, vitamins and minerals
Matters for health, fullness and how you feel while training.
Real but small once the rows above are in place.

blocks.title: In practice
paras: Many people turn this list upside down, worrying about supplements and meal timing while their total food and protein go unmeasured. If rows 1 and 2 are not handled, nothing below them will make up for it.

blocks.text: Calories are units of energy. Eating less than you use over time lowers your body mass. Eating more than you use raises it.

head: Goal
Energy position
rows: Eating below what you use, over time.
Eating a little above what you use, with enough protein and resistance training.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) states that fat loss is driven by a sustained calorie deficit, and that a wide range of diets, from low-fat to low-carbohydrate and ketogenic, can be similarly effective for body composition. {aragon2017}

The same paper says the apparent advantage of low-carbohydrate and ketogenic diets comes from their higher protein content. Intermittent fasting showed no significant advantage over daily calorie restriction. {aragon2017}
Its authors note a shortage of research in women and older people. {aragon2017}

blocks.text: So use the eating pattern you can sustain. The pattern delivers the calories and protein. It does not do anything special by itself.

head: Nutrient
Energy
Main role here
rows: Supplies amino acids for repair and building muscle.
A main fuel for repeated hard sets. Very low intake can show up as later sets fading.
Needed for absorbing some vitamins and for normal health. You need enough, not as much as possible.

blocks.text: A practical way to set your food: set protein first, because it has a clear target. Set fat next, at a level that keeps meals adequate and pleasant. Let carbohydrate fill the rest.

blocks.title: Carbohydrates are not the problem
paras: Carbohydrate restriction has no shown advantage once calories and protein are matched. {aragon2017} This matters in India: rice, roti, millets and dals are the affordable base of most meals. Cutting them out can hurt your training and make your diet harder to keep up.
The more useful question is how much total energy a meal gives you, and whether you are meeting your protein target.

blocks.text: [[protein|Protein]] covers this properly. In brief: 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg of body weight a day is sufficient for most exercising people, and your daily total comes first. {issnprotein} Common Indian sources include milk, curd, paneer, soya chunks, tofu, dals, rajma, chana, eggs where eaten, and whey where affordable.
The top three rows decide body composition. Row four decides how you feel on the way, and your health over decades. That is a different consideration, not a smaller one.

items: **Fibre.** WHO recommends adults get at least 25 g a day of naturally occurring fibre from food. Vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains supply it. {whocarb2023}
**Fruit and vegetables.** Eat a good range.
**Highly processed foods.** They are not forbidden. They are often high in calories and less filling, which can make a deficit harder to sustain. That is a practical argument, not a moral one.

blocks.title: Plant-based diets: nutrients that need attention
paras: A well-planned vegetarian or vegan diet can support training. Some nutrients need attention, especially on a fully plant-based diet:
**Vitamin B12.** Not reliably available from plant foods. Vegans need fortified foods or a supplement.
**Iron.** Iron from plants is less well absorbed. A vitamin C source with the meal helps, and tea or coffee with the meal can reduce absorption.
**Zinc.** Absorption is lower from diets high in phytate, found in whole grains and pulses.
**Omega-3.** The body converts only a limited amount from plant sources.
**Vitamin D.** For most people this depends more on sun exposure than on food.
If you suspect a deficiency, get a blood test and have a clinician interpret it. Do not guess and self-prescribe.

blocks.text: Drink across the day, and expect to need more in hot weather or when you sweat heavily. [[hydration|Hydration and electrolytes]] covers this properly.

One meal does not undo your progress, and one meal does not create it. Your body responds to what you do most weeks, over months. This does not mean intake does not matter. It means choosing the right timescale, and it argues against the all-or-nothing pattern that ends many diets.
When nutrition becomes a medical question

blocks.title: Get qualified support
paras: This Handbook does not diagnose, prescribe clinical diets or interpret medical results. See a qualified clinician or dietitian if any of these apply:
A condition affected by diet, such as diabetes, kidney or liver disease, coeliac disease, thyroid disorders, PCOS or heart disease.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding.
A suspected deficiency, or abnormal blood results.
Unintended weight loss, missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain. These may point to low energy availability, a medical concern.
Distress about food, eating or body weight, restriction that feels hard to control, or eating that affects your daily life. Asking early is easier than asking late.

items: Total energy, total protein and sticking with it account for most of the outcome.
A wide range of diets can work. Choose the one you can sustain.
Carbohydrate restriction has no shown advantage once calories and protein are matched.
Set protein first, then enough fat, then carbohydrate with the rest.

title: Calories and body composition
summary: Choosing a direction, and measuring whether it is working.

blocks.text: Body composition is the balance of muscle and fat in your body. It changes for two reasons: your training, and your energy intake. This chapter covers choosing a direction, setting a pace, estimating your starting point, and measuring the result well enough to know if it is working.

head: Goal
Energy position
What decides success
rows: Enough protein and continued training, so you lose mostly fat.
An underrated choice. Strength can still improve at a stable weight.
Keep it small. In practice, a big surplus mostly adds fat, because muscle grows slowly.

blocks.text: These are reasonable defaults, not research findings:

head: If you
Reasonable default
rows: Train and eat enough protein at about maintenance. Gaining muscle and losing fat together is most likely here.
Lose fat first. The ISSN says a larger deficit is more suitable at higher body fat. {aragon2017}
Are lean and want more muscle
Maintenance, with attention to protein and training. It gives you time to decide.

blocks.title: Every calorie estimate is a guess with a range
paras: Calculators give one confident number for your daily needs. Levlofit starts from an equation too. Individuals vary around any such estimate, and activity levels add more uncertainty. Treat the number as a starting guess, not a measurement.

blocks.text: Your own trend is more reliable. It takes two to three weeks:

items: Eat in a fairly consistent way and log it.
Weigh yourself in the same conditions most days: after waking, after using the toilet, before eating.
Compare one week's average with the next. A stable average means you are near maintenance, whatever the calculator said.
Adjust from there.

blocks.text: Daily body weight can swing by a kilogram or more from water, food in your gut, salt, carbohydrate and, for many women, the menstrual cycle. These swings are often larger than a week's real change, so one weigh-in tells you little.

blocks.title: The rule to use
paras: **Judge your weight by a seven-day average, not a single reading.** Average the last seven mornings and compare that week to week.

blocks.text: Weight also cannot separate muscle from fat. Track it along with your lifts, measurements, photos in consistent conditions, and how your clothes fit.
Use a percentage of your body weight, because the same kilograms mean very different things at different sizes.

head: Goal
Pace
How firm this is
rows: About 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week, slower as you get leaner
Moderate. One review found this pace may be better for keeping lean mass in lean, resistance-trained people. {helms2014}
Slow enough that weight rises over months, not weeks

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: Slower weight loss can better preserve lean mass in leaner people, and a larger deficit may suit those with higher body fat. Long-term success depends on sticking with it, which is another reason to avoid extreme deficits. Research in women and older people is limited. {aragon2017}

blocks.text: Gaining muscle and losing fat together
This is often called recomposition. It is real, and practical experience suggests it is more likely in certain situations:

items: You are new to resistance training.
You are returning after a long break.
You carry more body fat.
Your protein is adequate and your training is consistent. These are requirements, not boosters.

blocks.text: No reliable rate is established. As you train for longer, it usually gets slower and harder, and working on one goal at a time may become simpler.
You cannot choose where fat comes off

blocks.title: Spot reduction
paras: Training one body part is a poor way to lose fat from that area. Ab work builds your abs, but expect the fat over them to change as your overall body fat changes. Where you lose fat first is largely outside your control.

blocks.text: Use these practical responses after two to three weeks of data:

head: What you see

Add some food back. Faster is not better.

Your deficit may be too large or have run too long.

blocks.text: Adjust on trends, and change one thing at a time. Changing every week is usually too often to tell what worked.
When this stops being a food question

paras: Long or severe calorie restriction carries risks beyond your training plan. See a qualified clinician if you have:
Missed or irregular periods.
Frequent illness, lasting fatigue or repeated bone injuries.
Low sex drive, disturbed sleep or often feeling cold.
Distress about food or weight, restriction that feels hard to control, or eating that affects your daily life.
These are medical concerns. Asking for help early is easier than asking later.

items: **Treating a calculator as a measurement.** It is a starting guess.
**Judging progress on one weigh-in.** Daily swings often exceed weekly change.
**Cutting too hard.** It can cost muscle, training quality and your ability to keep going.
**Bulking hard.** Much of the excess is likely to be fat.
**Adjusting every few days.** That is too soon to separate signal from noise.
**Letting protein drop in a deficit.** It matters most when food is lowest.
Pick a direction and hold it long enough to judge. Maintenance is a fair choice.

blocks.text: Meal timing is oversold, though it is not nothing either. It helps in some situations. Those situations are narrower than the marketing claims, and wider than "it does not matter".

head: What
Effect
Grade
rows: Decides whether weight goes up or down
Helps decide how much of the change is muscle
Real, but secondary. Every 3 to 4 hours is the stated ideal
Matters when you need rapid recovery. Otherwise much less important

blocks.text: The claim is that you must have protein within about 30 minutes of training or the session is wasted. The position stands do not support that.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: The ISSN protein paper says the best time is likely a matter of what you tolerate, since benefits come from eating before or after training. The effect of exercise lasts at least 24 hours, though it likely fades with time. {issnprotein}

The ISSN timing paper says protein within two hours after exercise strongly stimulates muscle protein synthesis, and that the size and timing of your meal before training affects how much post-training protein matters. {kerksick2017}

blocks.text: So think in hours, not minutes, and remember the meal before training counts as well.
The goal is to feel fuelled and comfortable. Two patterns work:

items: **A normal meal a few hours before.** Protein and carbohydrate, with moderate fat and fibre so you are comfortable when you start.
**A lighter snack closer to training.** Mostly carbohydrate, with some protein, and low in fat and fibre.

blocks.text: Indian options include curd with fruit, poha or upma, oats with milk, a banana with milk, rice with dal, toast with peanut butter, and roti with paneer.
No exact timing is established. What feels comfortable varies with the person and the meal, so try it and see.

Training without food is a scheduling choice. In practice it suits some people and not others. If eating first makes you uncomfortable, train and eat afterwards. If you feel weak or light-headed, eat something small first. If that continues, or if you have diabetes or another medical condition, ask your doctor.
Have a meal with protein and carbohydrate within the next few hours. That is the whole recommendation.
You do not need a shake before leaving the gym. It is also fine if that is the easiest way to reach your daily protein.

blocks.title: When carbohydrate timing really matters
paras: Fast glycogen refuelling plans are for when you need rapid recovery, such as training twice in one day or competing on back-to-back days. {kerksick2017}
The ISSN paper says that outside such situations, when daily carbohydrate matches your needs, the importance of timed carbohydrate is "notably decreased". {kerksick2017}
If you train once a day, eat enough carbohydrate across the day and leave it there.

blocks.text: The number of meals is largely a practical choice. Changing meal frequency has shown limited effect on weight loss and body composition when not exercising, with stronger evidence for appetite and fullness. {kerksick2017}

**Training after a long gap without food, then blaming the plan.** Food belongs on your stall checklist.
**Eating a large, fatty, high-fibre meal right before training.** It can be uncomfortable.
**Trying new food on a day that matters.** Test it on an ordinary day first.
**Perfecting your timing while your daily total goes unmeasured.** Fix the big things first.
**Treating a post-workout shake as a requirement.** It is a convenience.

title: Eating well on a budget
summary: Hitting your targets for the least money.

blocks.text: A small budget changes which foods you use, not what your body needs. Total energy, protein and sticking with it still decide your result.

blocks.title: Practical guidance
paras: Prices and availability vary by city, season and household, so most of this chapter is practical advice rather than research. The protein figures come from food composition tables.

blocks.text: When money is tight, compare **cost per gram of protein**, not price per kilogram. Protein is usually the expensive part of your food, and carbohydrate is usually cheap.

blocks.title: Work it out once
paras: Divide the pack price by the grams of protein in the pack. Do this for the five or six sources you can actually buy. You only need to do it occasionally, and the cheapest food by weight is often not the cheapest protein.

blocks.text: Dry soya chunks and pulses often work out cheap per gram of protein, dairy often sits in the middle, and paneer, whey and meat are often more expensive. Check your own local prices, since this is a starting guess.

Rice, atta, oats, potatoes, bananas, and seasonal fruit and vegetables are usually inexpensive. For fat, peanuts, seeds and ordinary cooking oil do the job. If you have money left over, a wider range of vegetables and enough fruit will make your food more pleasant, and healthier.

items: **Buy dry staples in bulk** if you can store them. Rice, dal, soya chunks and oats keep well.
**Buy seasonal produce.** It is usually cheaper.

paras: Batch cooking is a main budget strategy, but it can be risky if handled carelessly, particularly with cooked rice and pulses in hot weather.
Cool cooked food quickly, refrigerate it promptly and reheat it thoroughly. Do not keep leftovers at room temperature for long. If your fridge is unreliable, cook smaller amounts more often.

items: **Assuming eating well must be expensive.** Soya chunks, dal, eggs and milk can be affordable.

**Skipping meals to save money.** It cuts energy, and can lead to overeating later.
**Paying for "fitness" branded food.** Compare its protein and price with ordinary food.
**Forgetting to count dal.** Protein already in your meals counts.
**Cutting protein first.** It is the part most likely to go when money is short, and one that matters most.
Your targets do not change with your budget. Your foods do.

blocks.text: Supplements come last in the order of importance, behind energy, protein, sticking with it, food quality and timing. For most people, the list worth buying is very short. It is not empty, though. Two have position stands behind them.
Ask yourself four questions. If any answer is no, your money is probably better spent elsewhere.

items: Am I training consistently, and progressing on something?
Am I reaching my protein target most days?
Does my total food match my goal?
Am I sleeping enough, and regularly?

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: The ISSN calls creatine monohydrate "the most effective ergogenic nutritional supplement currently available to athletes" for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training. {issncreatine}

**Dose:** once muscles are saturated, 3 to 5 g a day generally maintains stores. Some studies suggest larger athletes may need 5 to 10 g a day. The fastest way to raise stores is 5 g four times a day for 5 to 7 days, but you do not have to do this. {issncreatine}

**Safety:** the paper reports that short and long-term use, up to 30 g a day for 5 years, is safe and well tolerated in healthy people. It also reports that creatine either has no effect on or reduces injury, dehydration and cramping in athletes. {issncreatine}

items: **Buy monohydrate.** It is the form the ISSN paper is about, and usually a low-cost one.
**Take it daily at any time you will remember.** Stores build over time, so exact timing matters little.
**Expect a small weight gain at first.** Creatine holds a little water. Your seven-day average may step up.

blocks.title: The safety statement has a limit
paras: That safety evidence is for healthy people. If you have kidney disease, any other diagnosed condition, or take prescription medicine, ask a clinician first. Levlofit does not advise on supplements alongside disease.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong for endurance, moderate for strength
paras: The ISSN says caffeine "has been shown to acutely enhance various aspects of exercise performance in many but not all studies". Aerobic endurance shows the most consistent moderate to large benefit. Benefits for strength and muscular endurance are small to moderate. {issncaffeine}

**Dose:** 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight has consistently improved performance. The minimum may be as low as 2 mg per kg. Very high doses, such as 9 mg per kg, bring more side effects and do not seem to be needed. {issncaffeine}
**Timing:** most commonly about 60 minutes before exercise. {issncaffeine}
**Differences between people:** genes and your usual caffeine intake may change how you respond, including effects on sleep and anxiety. {issncaffeine}

blocks.title: Caffeine and sleep
paras: Sleep loss lowers performance. {craven2022} A dose before training that costs you sleep is a poor trade, so if you train in the evening, try less caffeine or none.

blocks.text: Coffee and tea contain caffeine, so you do not need a pre-workout product to get it. Blends that hide their doses cannot be judged.

This is food in a convenient form. The ISSN calls it a practical way to get enough protein, while noting you can meet your needs from whole foods. {issnprotein} Buy it if it makes your target easier to reach, and compare its cost per gram of protein with food first.
Vitamins and minerals: correct a deficiency, do not guess at one
These are general notes, not advice for you personally.

head: Supplement
When it makes sense
Note
rows: Needed on a fully plant-based diet.
No expected benefit if your levels are already fine.
When sun exposure is limited or your levels are low.
Correcting a deficiency makes sense. Taking excess does not.
**Do not self-prescribe.** Too much iron is harmful. Get a blood test and see a clinician.
When you eat little long-chain omega-3, particularly on plant-based diets.
As low-cost cover for a narrow diet.

blocks.title: Blood results
paras: Levlofit does not interpret blood results. The right order is a test, then a clinician's reading, then a dose if you need one. This matters even more during pregnancy or breastfeeding, with any diagnosed condition, or with prescription medicine.

blocks.text: These have no strong case behind them in this Handbook's sources. That is not proof they can never work, but the burden of proof sits with the product.

head: Product
Why not
rows: No strong reason to expect a meaningful change in your body composition.
Fat loss is driven by a calorie deficit. {aragon2017} If one contains caffeine, you are paying extra for caffeine.
Your liver and kidneys already do this job.
BCAAs and EAAs, if your protein is enough
Protein already supplies them, and the ISSN suggests whole foods with all essential amino acids. {issnprotein}
No strong reason to expect a benefit if your protein is adequate.
If a blend hides each ingredient's dose, it cannot be checked against evidence.

blocks.title: The label is not a guarantee
paras: Supplements are checked less strictly than medicines. Labels may be inaccurate, and contamination or undeclared ingredients can happen. This Handbook gives no figure for how common this is.
Prefer products with independent third-party testing, where available.
Prefer single ingredients with clear doses over blends.
Be sceptical of promises of fast or dramatic results, and of unofficial sellers.
If you are a tested athlete, use only certified products.

head: Claim
Standing
rows: Misleading. Training supplies the signal, and food and sleep support it. Creatine helps the training you can do. It does not replace it.
Not supported in healthy people. Kidney disease is a separate matter for your doctor. {issncreatine}
Not supported. Athlete studies reported no effect or less of both. {issncreatine}
False. Loading is faster. A daily dose gets there more slowly. {issncreatine}
False. It is concentrated food protein.
False. Plant extracts can be active and can interact with medicines.

items: Energy, protein, sticking with it and sleep come before any supplement.
Creatine monohydrate is the one most worth considering: 3 to 5 g a day, with a strong safety record in healthy people.
Caffeine works best for endurance, and less consistently for strength. Do not trade sleep for it.
Protein powder is convenient food. Compare it with real food on price.
Correct a confirmed deficiency. Do not guess at one.
Blends that hide their doses cannot be judged.

title: Hydration and electrolytes
summary: One number worth knowing, and two ways to get it wrong.

sources.kenefick2018: Kenefick RW. Drinking strategies: planned drinking versus drinking to thirst. Sports Med 2018;48:31-37. doi:10.1007/s40279-017-0844-6

blocks.text: One common claim says drink constantly and hit a fixed daily target. Another says thirst handles everything. The evidence is more contextual. Past a certain point, losing fluid impairs performance. Thirst is a good guide in some conditions and a poor one in others. And drinking too much can be dangerous.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: Dehydration of 2% of body mass or more is associated with poorer temperature control, more strain on the heart and, in many conditions, poorer aerobic performance. These conditions include warmer, longer and more intense exercise. In 34 endurance studies with 60 observations, 68% showed significantly impaired performance at this level. {kenefick2018}
Many of these studies were done in a laboratory, which may not match real conditions. {kenefick2018}

blocks.text: Two per cent of body mass is 1.4 kg for a 70 kg person. Body mass losses this large take time to build up. {kenefick2018} This figure concerns aerobic work. It is **not established** that the same threshold applies to resistance training.

Thirst is a real signal, with a known limit: it tends to ease before you are fully rehydrated. In one study people drinking freely replaced about half of what they lost. When you sweat a lot, that deficit can build up. {kenefick2018}

head: Situation
Strategy
rows: Exercise under about 60 to 90 minutes, in cooler conditions or at lower intensity
Drinking to thirst may be enough. {kenefick2018}
Exercise over 90 minutes, especially in heat
Heavy sweating, or sessions where performance matters
Planned drinking. Find your sweat rate. {kenefick2018}
Indian summer heat, or a gym without air conditioning
In practice, treat this like the hot case, however short the session.

blocks.title: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
paras: Drinking far more than your body can get rid of dilutes the sodium in your blood. This is mainly a risk in long endurance events rather than gym training, and it can be life-threatening.
Its symptoms can look like dehydration: headache, nausea, confusion and dizziness. Swollen hands or face are also warning signs. Drinking more can make it worse.
**A clear rule: never drink so much that you gain weight during exercise.** {kenefick2018}
Suspected hyponatremia is a medical emergency. Get urgent medical care.

blocks.text: If you train long, hard or in heat, one session can replace a lot of guessing. This is a practical method, and it estimates fluid lost. It does not precisely measure how hydrated you are.

items: Weigh yourself just before training, in minimal clothing.
Note everything you drink during the session.
Weigh yourself again right after, towelled dry, in the same clothing.
Weight lost plus fluid drunk is roughly your fluid loss. One kilogram is about one litre. {kenefick2018}

blocks.text: Try it once in cool conditions and once in heat to learn your own range.

Needs vary with your body size, climate, activity and the water in your food, so no single number fits everyone. Levlofit shows a daily water goal, and you can set your own. Treat it as a reminder, not a rule. In practice:

items: Drink across the day. Tea, coffee, milk, dal and curd count too.
Drink more in heat and around longer or harder sessions.
Start sessions hydrated.
Replace fluid over the hours after a session, not all at once.

blocks.text: **Urine colour** is a rough check. Pale yellow suggests you are drinking enough, and consistently dark suggests otherwise. Some vitamins and medicines can change it.
Electrolytes are minerals in your body fluids, involved in fluid balance and in nerve and muscle function.

head: Electrolyte
Why it matters for training
rows: The main one lost in sweat, and the one involved in hyponatremia.
Lost in smaller amounts. Fruit, vegetables, dal and milk supply it.
Lost in small amounts. Important in your diet, but rarely a hydration concern.

blocks.title: Cramp
paras: Cramp is often blamed on electrolyte loss or dehydration. A competing view blames nerve and muscle fatigue. This is **contested**, so do not assume electrolytes will prevent it. Frequent or severe cramps, or cramps at rest, need a clinician.

blocks.text: Do you need a sports drink?

head: Situation
What is enough
rows: Ordinary gym session in normal conditions
Long session, heavy sweating or real heat
Fluid with some salt. Nimbu paani with salt, or an ORS-style drink, can do this cheaply.
Remember that sports drinks contain calories.

blocks.text: If you have high blood pressure, or kidney or heart disease, ask your doctor about added salt.

items: **Treating a daily target as a requirement.** No one number fits everyone.
**Assuming thirst is always enough.** It becomes less reliable as time, heat and sweat rise.
**Assuming more is always safer.** Never finish heavier than you started.
**Buying sports drinks for a short gym session.** Water usually does the job.
**Trying to fix hydration during a session.** Start hydrated instead.
**Blaming every cramp on electrolytes.** That can delay finding the real cause.
Dehydration of 2% of body mass or more is linked with poorer aerobic performance.
For shorter, cooler or lighter sessions, drinking to thirst may be enough.
Longer, hotter and harder sessions need planned drinking.
Never gain weight during exercise. Suspected hyponatremia is an emergency.
Sodium is the electrolyte lost most in sweat. The link between cramps and electrolytes is contested.

title: Eating out, travel and occasions
summary: How not to lose your progress over nothing.

sources.aragon2017: Aragon AA et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets and body composition. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:16. doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0174-y

blocks.text: Restaurants, travel, weddings and festivals are a permanent part of life. A way of eating that only works in your own kitchen will not last.
The ISSN says the long-term success of a diet depends on sticking with it. {aragon2017} So how you handle the exceptions matters. The advice below is practical judgement, not research.

head: Timescale
What it tells you
rows: Very little, against a week or a month.
The shortest span worth reacting to.
Where your body composition really responds.

blocks.text: One large restaurant meal is only a part of a week's food. The bigger cost often comes from your reaction to it.

You may hear that 80% of your meals should be nutritious and 20% flexible. The idea is sound: most of your food should serve your goals, and some can be flexible. The exact ratio is a memory aid, not a finding. Build a week that mostly works, and stop auditing the exceptions.
You are usually choosing from someone else's options, so aim for the best available choice.

head: What to do
How
rows: Paneer, dal, chana, curd, eggs, chicken, fish or tofu. Restaurant meals often have plenty of energy and less protein.
Deep-fried dishes and rich gravies usually have far more calories than tandoori, grilled, roasted or dry versions.
Sugary drinks, juice and alcohol add calories with little fullness.
Sharing, or stopping when comfortable, often works better than deciding beforehand to eat half.
A salad, raita or vegetable side can replace some richer food.

blocks.title: Do not arrive starving
paras: Skipping meals to "save" calories for an event can backfire and lead to eating more. Eat normally through the day, with protein, then enjoy the event.

items: **It contains calories,** without much fullness, so they are easy to miss.
**Mixers add more,** especially soft drinks and juices.
**It can disturb your sleep,** even if it makes you drowsy.
**It can loosen your food decisions** during and after drinking.

blocks.text: Levlofit makes no health recommendation about drinking. That is a personal and medical matter. If your progress has stalled and alcohol is regular, count it before you decide your plan has failed.

items: **Carry protein.** Roasted chana, peanuts, whey in a shaker, or milk cartons where available.
**Carry water.** Travel days make it easy to drink too little.
**Do not skip meals because the options are imperfect.** An imperfect meal usually beats a missed one.
**Expect your weight to move for reasons other than fat.** Salt, fluid, fibre and timing all change. Your seven-day average will smooth this out.
**Walk.** Travel is otherwise very still.

blocks.text: A missed week of training does not undo months of work. The bigger risk is returning at your old loads straight away, so ease back in.
Indian festival seasons can be long and full of food. Treating each one as a threat is miserable and unnecessary.

items: Eat normally, with protein, during the day.
Eat what you want at the occasion.
Return to your usual pattern at the **next meal**, not next Monday.
Do not punish yourself with extra exercise or restriction afterwards.

blocks.title: Compensation is the pattern to watch
paras: Skipping meals before an event, exercising to "cancel" food, restricting hard the next day, or feeling a lot of guilt about a meal can turn an ordinary occasion into a problem.

These can also be early signs of a difficult relationship with food. If the pattern continues, feels hard to control or affects your daily life, talk to a qualified clinician or dietitian. This Handbook does not diagnose or treat eating disorders.

blocks.text: Hostel mess, conference food, long journeys, family obligations. In order of usefulness:

items: Take the protein that is available.
Add vegetables or fruit, if there are any.
Drink water, not sweetened drinks.
Eat until comfortable, not full.
Stop thinking about it afterwards.
**Believing one meal matters.** Over a month, it matters little.
**Skipping meals beforehand.** It can make you eat more overall.
**Declaring a "cheat day".** One flexible meal can grow into a whole day.
**Giving up on the week after one meal.** This costs far more than the meal.
**Punishing yourself with exercise.** Training is not a payment for food.
**Forgetting drinks.** They can add up quickly.
**Reacting to the scale after travel.** Wait for your average.
Your body responds over months. One meal is small, and your reaction can cost more.
80/20 is a memory aid, not a finding.
Eating out: find the protein, notice the oil, count your drinks and do not arrive starving.
Alcohol adds calories and can disturb your sleep.
Travelling: carry protein and water, and ignore the scale for a few days.
Watch for compensating. Get support if it becomes a pattern.

summary: This volume in one place, with the evidence attached.
