blocks.text: This chapter gathers the volume's corrections. Each answer says what supports it. Where the evidence is thin or divided, it says so.

head: Claim
Answer
rows: False. Fat loss is driven by a calorie deficit, and a wide range of diets can work. {aragon2017}
"Eating after a certain hour causes fat gain."
Not supported as a rule. Your total intake over weeks decides your direction. {aragon2017}
Overstated. Limiting added sugar is sensible, but you do not need to eliminate it.
False. One meal is small against a month.
"You can lose fat from one chosen area."
Do not rely on it. Fat loss in an area generally follows overall fat loss.

head: Claim
Answer
rows: "The body can only use 30 g of protein per meal."

Not what the ISSN says. It gives 20 to 40 g as a general dose to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, and says the findings are mixed. It does not set that as a limit on what you can use. {issnprotein}
If you have kidney disease, your protein is a matter for your doctor. Levlofit does not advise on it.
Not supported. Plant protein research is limited, but rice protein matched whey in one 8-week study. {issnprotein}
False. It is a practical option, and needs can be met from food. {issnprotein}
Not shown. 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg is sufficient for most exercising people. Evidence above 3.0 g per kg is novel. {issnprotein}

head: Claim
Answer
rows: "You must eat within 30 minutes of training."
False. The effect of exercise lasts at least 24 hours, and eating before or after both help. {issnprotein}
"You must eat every two to three hours."
Partly. The number of meals has limited effect on weight loss and body composition when not exercising. {kerksick2017} Spreading protein every 3 to 4 hours is the stated ideal. {issnprotein}
"Training without eating burns more fat, or ruins muscle."
Treat it as a scheduling choice. Eat first if you feel weak or light-headed.
Depends. Timed carbohydrate matters less unless you need rapid recovery. {kerksick2017}

head: Claim
Answer
rows: Not supported in healthy people, including up to 30 g a day for 5 years. Kidney disease is a separate matter for your doctor. {issncreatine}
Not supported. Athlete studies reported no effect or less of both. {issncreatine}
False. Loading is faster, and a daily dose gets there more slowly. {issncreatine}
Overstated. Endurance shows the most consistent benefit. Benefits for strength are small to moderate. {issncaffeine}
False. Fat loss comes from a calorie deficit. {aragon2017}
"BCAAs help if you already eat enough protein."
Little reason to expect it. Protein already contains them.
False. Plant extracts can be active and can interact with medicines.

head: Claim
Answer
rows: "Everyone should drink a fixed amount of water a day."
No one number fits everyone. Treat your water goal as a reminder.
"Waiting until you are thirsty is always a mistake."
False for shorter, cooler or lighter sessions. It falls short when you sweat heavily. {kenefick2018}
False. Drinking too much can be dangerous. Never gain weight during exercise. {kenefick2018}
Contested. Frequent or severe cramps, or cramps at rest, need a clinician.
"You need a sports drink for a gym session."
Usually not. Water covers most ordinary sessions.

head: Question
Answer
rows: How often should I weigh myself?
Most days, in the same conditions. Judge by your seven-day average.
Should I eat before the gym?
Often helpful, not required. Find what feels comfortable.
How do I know my maintenance calories?
Eat consistently for two to three weeks and compare weekly averages.
How fast should I lose fat?
About 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week is a reasonable pace, slower as you get leaner. {helms2014}
Can I gain muscle and lose fat together?
Often, especially if you are new, returning or carrying more body fat. No reliable rate is established.
Mostly no. Creatine is worth considering, and caffeine depends on you.
Is a vegetarian or vegan diet a disadvantage?
It can work with more attention to protein and variety. On a fully plant-based diet, B12 needs a supplement or fortified food.
Should I get a blood test before taking vitamins or minerals?
Yes, then have a clinician read it. Some are harmful in excess.
My weight jumped 2 kg overnight. What happened?
Most likely water, food, salt, carbohydrate or digestion. Your seven-day average will smooth it out.
I have a medical condition. Does this apply to me?
Treat it as general education only, and get advice from a qualified clinician or dietitian.

items: Energy sets your direction. Protein helps decide how much is muscle. Sticking with it decides whether either happens.
Aim for about 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg a day, across your meals. {issnprotein}
A wide range of diets can work. Use one you will follow. {aragon2017}
Timing is a refinement.
Creatine, and possibly caffeine. Very little else.
Judge progress by your seven-day average, over months.
Did each main meal have a protein source?
Was my food about right for my current goal?
Did I include vegetables and fruit?
Did I drink across the day, and more in the heat?
Did I ignore any one day's number on the scale?
Many nutrition arguments are about things that barely matter.
Check what supports a claim before you act on it, including the claims in this Handbook.
Simple habits kept for years beat perfect ones kept for weeks.

title: Sleep
summary: What sleep does, and which sleep advice holds up when tested.

sources.aasm2015: Watson NF et al. Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult: a joint consensus statement of the AASM and SRS. J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11(6):591-592.
sources.cunha2023: Cunha LA et al. The impact of sleep interventions on athletic performance: a systematic review. Sports Med Open 2023;9(1):58.
sources.issncaffeine: Guest NS et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2021;18:1.
sources.dobrosielski2021: Dobrosielski DA et al. The association between poor sleep and the incidence of sport and physical training-related injuries in adult athletic populations: a systematic review. Sports Med 2021;51(4):777-793. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01416-3
sources.craven2022: Craven J et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytical review. Sports Med 2022;52(11):2669-2690. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y

blocks.text: [[recovery|Recovery]] shows what sleep loss costs you. This chapter looks the other way: how much sleep is recommended, what happens when you sleep more on purpose, and which familiar sleep advice has evidence behind it.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong, by consensus
paras: A joint statement from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society supports 7 or more hours a night, regularly, for adults aged 18 to 60. {aasm2015}

blocks.text: Notice that this is a floor, not a range. Seven hours is the minimum to aim for. If you often wake unrested after seven, try more.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, from limited studies
paras: A review of 25 sleep intervention studies in athletes found that sleeping longer at night and napping were the most effective of the methods tested for improving performance. The authors acknowledge the limited amount of high-quality evidence. {cunha2023}

blocks.text: You cannot decide to fall asleep. You can decide to be in bed earlier. If you are often short of sleep, this is likely to be the most useful change in this chapter.

blocks.title: The standard advice has thin support in athletes
paras: The same review found sleep hygiene advice and removing electronic devices at night had no effect on sleep and later performance. These results come from only a few studies. {cunha2023}

items: **Do not stop these habits if they help you.** They are free, and a few studies do not prove they never work.
**Do not expect much from them alone.** If your sleep is truly poor, a neater bedtime routine may not be the fix.
**Put your effort into time in bed.** That has better support.

head: Habit
Standing
rows: Sensible. Caffeine can affect sleep, and this varies between people. {issncaffeine}
Removing devices showed no effect in a few athlete studies. Keep it if it helps you. {cunha2023}
It can make you drowsy and still disturb your sleep.

blocks.text: The same review found naps among the most effective methods overall. {cunha2023} A nap is a reasonable option if you are short of sleep. It does not replace your night's sleep. Keep it early enough that it does not push back your bedtime, and if you nap before a session, notice whether you actually perform better.

You will often hear that poor sleep causes injury. A review of 12 cohort studies concluded that current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for injury in adult athletes, and that the studies were too mixed to settle the question. {dobrosielski2021}
The case for sleep rests on performance, and that is strong enough.

In a large review, sleep loss lowered exercise performance by about 7.6% on average. Afternoon and evening sessions consistently suffered, while morning sessions were largely unaffected. If a bad night is unavoidable and your session cannot move, train earlier if you can. {craven2022}

The consensus recommendation is for regular sleep. {aasm2015} It is **not established** that weekend catch-up fully reverses a week of short nights. Treat extra sleep as useful and partial: better than nothing, and worse than not building the debt.
When poor sleep is a medical problem

blocks.title: See a clinician
paras: If your sleep stays bad, more routine tips may not be the answer, and looking for them may delay real help. See a qualified clinician if you have:
Trouble falling or staying asleep over several weeks, despite enough time in bed.
Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping or choking in your sleep, or waking unrefreshed after long sleep.
Overwhelming daytime sleepiness, or falling asleep without meaning to.
Sleep problems alongside lasting low mood, anxiety or loss of interest.
Restless, uncomfortable feelings in your legs at night.
Insomnia and other sleep disorders are medical conditions with treatments. Levlofit does not diagnose them or recommend sleep medicine.

items: **Treating seven hours as the whole target.** The statement says 7 or more.
**Perfecting the routine instead of the duration.** Time in bed has better support.
**Expecting routine changes to fix real insomnia.** If they have not worked in a few weeks, see a clinician.
**Napping into the evening.** It can eat into your night's sleep.
**Using injury claims as motivation.** The performance case is real without them.
Aim for 7 or more hours a night, regularly.
Spending longer in bed is the change with the better support.
Naps can help. They do not replace your night's sleep.
Sleep hygiene and removing devices showed no effect in a few athlete studies.
It is not established that poor sleep alone causes injury.
Sleep problems that last deserve a clinician.

title: Stress management
summary: Stress mostly costs you sessions.

sources.stults2014: Stults-Kolehmainen MA, Sinha R. The effects of stress on physical activity and exercise. Sports Med 2014;44:81-121. doi:10.1007/s40279-013-0090-5
sources.noetel2024: Noetel M et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ 2024;384:e075847.
sources.craven2022: Craven J et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytical review. Sports Med 2022;52(11):2669-2690. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y
sources.telemanas2024: Press Information Bureau, Government of India. Tele MANAS: Revolutionizing Mental Health Care in India. October 2024. static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2024/oct/doc20241013415701.pdf

blocks.text: Stress is usually described as something that slows your recovery. The better-supported effect is simpler: **stress makes you less likely to train at all**. That changes what you should do about it.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate to strong for the effect on behaviour
paras: Of 55 prospective studies, 76.4% found that psychological stress predicted less physical activity or more sitting. Among higher-quality studies, it was 85.7%. {stults2014}

Some studies, 18.2%, found the opposite, with stress leading to more exercise. The authors note that habitually active people exercise more under stress, while those just starting exercise less. {stults2014}

blocks.title: The most useful point in this chapter
paras: The habit itself can protect you. The early work of making training automatic may be what keeps you going through stressful periods later.

blocks.text: What this chapter does not claim

It is **not established** here that stress directly slows your physical recovery between sessions. It is plausible, and stress can disturb your sleep, which does affect performance. None of the advice below depends on that claim.

Exercise may also help how you feel. A large review of trials found walking, jogging, yoga and strength training eased depression, with effects that seemed comparable to some established treatments, though with less confidence in the evidence. {noetel2024} That is useful. It does not make training a replacement for care. For stress specifically, the review above found only early evidence that stress management combined with exercise protects activity levels. {stults2014}

head: Area
What happens
Standing
rows: Harder to fall or stay asleep.
Practical observation. Sleep loss then affects performance. {craven2022}
Eating much more or less, and less regularly.
You attend, but train less hard.

blocks.text: Let your training move with your life. Cutting sets for a demanding month and restoring them later keeps you consistent. Keeping the same plan and missing sessions does not. Levlofit can make a day lighter or move a session, or offer fewer days if you keep missing them.

head: Instead of
Try this
rows: Cut your sets and keep your schedule.
Do your first, most important exercise, and let the smaller ones go.
Shorten the session rather than cancelling it.

blocks.text: If performance is falling across several exercises, add stress to your checklist, alongside sleep and food.
These are ordinary, low-cost habits, not tested training methods.

items: **Protect your sleep first.** Think time in bed.
**Keep training scheduled, at lower volume.** The habit protects you.
**Keep meals regular.** Protein and total food can slip during hard weeks.
**Cut other commitments before training,** if you can.
**Take breaks** during long work or study, get outdoors when possible, and talk to people you trust.
**Slow your breathing** when you feel overwhelmed.

blocks.title: Beyond a training handbook
paras: Talk to a qualified mental health professional, a doctor or someone you trust if you have:
Low mood, anxiety or loss of interest in things you enjoy, lasting for weeks.
Feeling overwhelmed in a way that affects your daily life, relationships, work or study.
Sleep problems that continue despite enough time in bed.
Large changes in appetite or weight that you did not intend.
Using alcohol or other substances to manage how you feel.
Training that feels compulsive: distress at missing a session, training through illness or injury, or exercising to make up for food.
Thoughts of harming yourself. Do not wait. In India, you can call Tele-MANAS on 14416 at any time, or your local emergency services. {telemanas2024}
Levlofit does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions. Asking for support is not a failure of discipline.

items: **Dropping training first.** It is often the easiest thing to cancel.
**Keeping full volume and missing sessions.** Cut back on purpose instead.
**Treating a stressful month as a plan failure.** Diagnose before you change anything.
**Expecting training to fix a medical problem.** It may help. It does not replace care.
In most prospective studies, stress predicted less activity.
People just starting tend to lose sessions to stress. Habitually active people often train more.
Reduce on purpose and keep your schedule, rather than missing weeks.
Exercise may help your mood, and it does not replace care.
Lasting low mood, anxiety, compulsive training or thoughts of self-harm need qualified support.

title: Mobility and flexibility
summary: You may already be training your mobility without knowing it.

sources.ingram2025: Ingram LA et al. Mechanisms underlying range of motion improvements following acute and chronic static stretching: a systematic review, meta-analysis and multivariate meta-regression. Sports Med 2025;55:1449-1466. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02204-7

blocks.text: [[warmup-mobility|Warm-up and mobility]] covers what stretching does. This chapter asks the practical question: if you already lift, how much separate mobility work do you need? Often less than you might think.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The range you can reach and control at a joint. It needs strength through that range.
The range available at a joint, usually measured passively.

blocks.text: Stretching does not make muscles longer. Fascicle length did not change after one session or many. Stiffness fell, and with repeated stretching, tolerance to the stretch rose. {ingram2025}
Resistance training improves range of motion

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A review of 55 studies found that resistance training increased range of motion (effect size 0.73). It showed no significant difference from stretching (0.08, p = 0.79). Combining the two did no better than stretching alone (-0.001, p = 0.99). The authors conclude that stretching before or after resistance training may not be necessary to improve flexibility. {alizadeh2023}
Untrained and sedentary people gained more (1.042) than trained or active people (0.43). Using only body mass did not significantly improve range. {alizadeh2023}

blocks.title: What this means for you
paras: If you train with external load through a full range, a separate stretching routine may add little. Full range on your working sets can also be part of your mobility work, so cutting depth to add load costs you twice.

blocks.text: When dedicated mobility work is worth it

items: **A position you cannot reach limits an exercise you want,** such as squat depth or a comfortable overhead position.
**You cannot yet load the range at all.** You may need to open it first.
**You train only with bodyweight.** The result above may not apply to you. {alizadeh2023}
**You want range for something outside lifting.** A sport, an activity or comfort. That is a fair personal reason.

blocks.text: Otherwise, a general daily stretching routine is a habit you may enjoy, not something you need.

head: Approach
Effect on jumping and sprinting
rows: Improved jump height and sprint time. {li2023}

blocks.text: These studies measured explosive tasks, so the effect on an ordinary set may differ.
**In practice:** if a static stretch helps you reach a position, use it, then do dynamic movement and warm-up sets. Without such a limit, skip it.

head: Area
What it can limit
Standing
rows: Mechanically clear. Specific drills are not tested here.
Not established that ankle drills change results. Test your own depth.
Mechanically clear. Specific drills are not tested here.
Often stiffness and tolerance. Loaded hinging through a full range is a good place to start. {alizadeh2023}

items: **Pick a routine you will keep up.** One review found hold time and frequency played little role in how much range people gained. {konrad2024}
**Load the range you gain,** so you can use it. {alizadeh2023}
**Target the real limit.** A muscle can feel tight without being what limits you.
**Expect months.** A warm-up uses range you already have.

blocks.text: Here is a practical example, if your squat depth is limited and nothing hurts:

head: Step
What to do
rows: Film your depth from the side, with the camera in the same place each time.
Squat under load to your full available depth, every session.
Add ankle and hip work before the session if it lets you reach further that day.
After six to eight weeks, not weekly.

blocks.text: If your depth has not moved after a couple of months, ask a qualified professional whether something structural is limiting you.
What this chapter does not claim

blocks.title: Mobility and injury
paras: It is **not established** that mobility work prevents injury. The stronger evidence for lower injury risk is strength training itself, in sports groups. {lauersen2018} Train mobility because it lets you do exercises you otherwise could not.

blocks.title: Stretching into pain
paras: Mild discomfort is expected. Sharp, radiating or joint-line pain is not. Stop, and see a qualified clinician rather than stretching harder.

items: **Doing a general daily routine and expecting more range.** If you already lift through a full range, it may add little. {alizadeh2023}
**Cutting range on working sets, then stretching to fix it.** Your working sets could be doing that job.
**Stretching whatever feels tight.** Tightness is a feeling, not a diagnosis.
**Testing weekly.** Change takes months.
**Expecting a warm-up to build range.** It uses what you have.
**Forcing a painful position.** Stop instead.
Resistance training with load improved range of motion about as well as stretching.
Full range on your working sets helps your mobility.
Stretching lowers stiffness and raises tolerance. It does not lengthen muscle.
Dedicated work suits a specific limit, bodyweight-only training or goals outside lifting.
Avoid static stretching alone right before explosive work.
It is not established that mobility work prevents injury.

title: Muscle soreness
summary: Reducing the pain is not the same as speeding up recovery.

sources.wiecha2025: Wiecha S et al. Physical therapies for delayed-onset muscle soreness: an umbrella and mapping systematic review with meta-meta-analysis. Sports Med 2025;55:1183-1212. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02187-5
sources.damas2016: Damas F et al. Resistance training-induced changes in integrated myofibrillar protein synthesis are related to hypertrophy only after attenuation of muscle damage. J Physiol 2016;594(18):5209-5222. doi:10.1113/JP272472
sources.aasm2015: Watson NF et al. Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult: a joint consensus statement of the AASM and SRS. J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11(6):591-592.

blocks.text: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is the ache that appears a day or two after unfamiliar or hard exercise. The review below describes it as coming from intense, unaccustomed exercise. {wiecha2025} It tells you less about your training than many people assume.
This chapter separates three questions: what soreness is, what reduces it, and whether reducing it does anything for your training.

Soreness usually peaks a day or two after a session, and it is most likely after unfamiliar work: a new plan, a return after a break, a new exercise or a jump in volume. Its exact cause is not settled, and nothing practical here depends on settling it.

Repeat the same session a week or two later and you will usually be less sore, even with the same or more work. So soreness mostly tells you the work was unfamiliar. It does not tell you the work was productive.
Soreness is not a progress signal

blocks.title: In practice
paras: A productive session after months of training may leave you barely sore. A new session can leave you very sore and still give you little. Chasing soreness adds recovery cost. Judge your sessions by your logged performance over weeks.

blocks.text: There is also evidence behind this. In one small study, muscle damage peaked early in training and was not related to later growth. {damas2016}

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate for direction, with a serious quality warning
paras: A review of 29 systematic reviews, covering 863 trials and 24 treatments, reported effects on soreness at various time points from cooling therapy, cryostimulation, contrast therapy, massage, phototherapy and kinesiotaping. Evidence for stretching, exercise and electrical stimulation was weak. {wiecha2025}
**Seventeen of the 29 reviews were of critically low quality, and only two were high quality.** The authors say the evidence has uncertainties and weaknesses. {wiecha2025}

blocks.title: Less pain is not the same as better results
paras: These findings are about soreness, a feeling. They do not show that a treatment speeds up your performance recovery or improves your results. Feeling better is a fair goal. It is just a different goal.

blocks.text: Probably the most practical way to limit soreness is not on those lists: **progress gradually, so the work is rarely unfamiliar.**
What has weak support for soreness

head: Common advice
Standing
rows: Weak evidence for soreness. It is still reasonable for other reasons. {wiecha2025}
Not established. Protein matters for other reasons.

head: Situation
Reasonable response
rows: Moderate soreness, technique or range affected
Lower the load and keep a full range.
Train something else or cut back a lot. Then ask whether your volume rose too quickly.
Sore in the same area for weeks
This is unlikely to be ordinary soreness. See below.

blocks.text: These are practical signs, not a diagnosis.

head: More like soreness
Get it checked
rows: Appears hours to a day or two later
Came on suddenly, during the session
Sharp, stabbing or in one spot
Both sides, if both were trained
One side or one specific point
Limited movement, joint involved or swelling

blocks.title: Urgent: when soreness is not soreness
paras: Rarely, severe muscle damage after extreme or unaccustomed exercise causes rhabdomyolysis. Muscle contents enter the blood and can damage the kidneys. It is a medical emergency.
Get urgent medical care if severe muscle pain comes with:
**Dark, cola or tea-coloured urine.**
Marked swelling of the muscles.
Weakness far beyond normal soreness, or being unable to use the limb.
Passing little urine, nausea, confusion or fever.
This does not mean you should worry about ordinary soreness. It means knowing the one picture that needs immediate attention.

items: **Sleep:** 7 or more hours. {aasm2015}
**Enough food and protein.**
**Gradual progress.**
**Fluid across the day.**
**Ordinary movement.** It is fine for its own sake.
**Using soreness as your score.** It mostly reflects novelty.
**Chasing it.** That adds recovery cost.
**Assuming less pain means faster recovery.** The evidence is about soreness.
**Stopping all movement.** Reducing is reasonable. You rarely need to stop.
**Testing sore muscles with heavy loads.** That is a poor day to find out.
**Raising volume so quickly you are badly sore again and again.** Slow down.
Soreness reflects unfamiliar work more than productive work, and it fades with repetition.
Cooling, massage, contrast therapy, phototherapy and kinesiotaping showed effects on soreness.
Evidence for stretching, exercise and electrical stimulation is weak.
Most of the underlying reviews were low quality, so hold this loosely.
Less pain is not proof of faster recovery or better results.
Severe pain with dark urine is an emergency.

title: Recovery tools
summary: Most change how you feel. One can lower your results.

sources.malta2021: Malta ES et al. The effects of regular cold-water immersion use on training-induced changes in strength and endurance performance: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med 2021;51(1):161-174. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01362-0
sources.wiecha2025: Wiecha S et al. Physical therapies for delayed-onset muscle soreness: an umbrella and mapping systematic review with meta-meta-analysis. Sports Med 2025;55:1183-1212. doi:10.1007/s40279-025-02187-5

blocks.text: Recovery tools are sold on a promise: use them and you will adapt faster. Several have evidence for making you less sore, which is a smaller claim. And one popular tool has evidence of harming the strength gains you train for, so it comes first.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, and negative for strength
paras: A review of eight articles on regular cold-water immersion, at 15 °C or below, alongside training found a harmful effect on one-repetition maximum, maximum isometric strength and strength endurance (effect size -0.60, -0.87 to -0.33). It did not appear to affect aerobic performance. {malta2021}

blocks.title: What this means for you
paras: If you lift to get stronger, do not make cold-water immersion after sessions a routine habit. You may be trading less soreness for smaller strength gains.
It may be a fair trade when you must perform again soon, such as during a tournament. Treat that as a deliberate choice, not a default.

blocks.text: A quick cold shower because you like it is not what was studied.

head: Question
What the evidence says
rows: For several tools, yes, from a large but weak literature. {wiecha2025}
Does it speed up performance recovery?
Not established here for these tools.
Does it improve your training results?
No tool here has shown this. Regular cold-water immersion had a harmful effect on strength. {malta2021}

head: Tool
Soreness
Verdict
rows: The foundation, with direct performance evidence. {craven2022}
May help by reducing unfamiliar work
Showed effects at some time points. {wiecha2025}
Occasional use. It has a cold part, and it was not tested in the strength review.
Showed effects at some time points. {wiecha2025}
Not separately reported in the summary used here
No significant performance benefit in warm-ups. {li2023} Use it for comfort.
Useful for range, not as a recovery tool.
Avoid as a routine if you lift for strength. {malta2021}

blocks.text: Remember the warning from [[muscle-soreness|Muscle soreness]]: 17 of those 29 reviews were of critically low quality. {wiecha2025}
Deciding whether a tool is worth it

items: **Are sleep, food and training volume handled?** If not, no tool will make up for them.
**What are you buying?** Usually feeling better. That is fine, as long as you know it.
**What does it cost?** Money, time and, for regular cold immersion, possibly strength gains.

blocks.title: In practice
paras: If a tool makes you feel better and you enjoy it, use it. That can help you keep turning up. Just do not spend money expecting results no evidence has promised.

items: **Anything promising faster recovery.** No tool here has shown it.
**A long routine after every session.** You will likely drop it.
**A wearable recovery score that overrules your log.** Treat it as a weak input.
**Supplements sold for recovery.** They do not replace sleep or food.

blocks.title: Use these tools sensibly
paras: **Cold immersion** carries risks from sudden cold and from staying in too long. If you have a heart condition, ask a clinician first. Do not immerse alone in open water.
**Saunas and hot baths** carry risks with dehydration, alcohol, pregnancy and some medical conditions.
**Massage guns and deep pressure** should not be used over an injury, joint, bone or the neck, or over an area that is numb, swollen or painful.
**Compression** is not right for everyone, especially with circulation problems or a history of blood clots.
If you have a diagnosed condition, ask a clinician before trying any of these.

items: **Routine cold plunges after lifting.** See above.
**Buying tools before fixing sleep and food.**
**Reading "less soreness" as "faster recovery".** They are different claims.
**Ranking every recovery method on one scale.** Sleep and a massage gun are not the same kind of thing.
Sleep, food and sensible training volume come first. The rest is optional.
Several tools reduce soreness, on weak evidence.
Regular cold-water immersion harmed strength gains. Do not make it a routine if you lift for strength.
Foam rolling and massage guns are fine for comfort.
Feeling better is a fair reason to use something. Just call it that.

title: Motivation and mental recovery
summary: What the evidence says about wanting to train.

sources.teixeira2012: Teixeira PJ et al. Exercise, physical activity, and self-determination theory: a systematic review. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 2012;9:78. doi:10.1186/1479-5868-9-78
sources.craven2022: Craven J et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytical review. Sports Med 2022;52(11):2669-2690. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y
sources.stults2014: Stults-Kolehmainen MA, Sinha R. The effects of stress on physical activity and exercise. Sports Med 2014;44:81-121. doi:10.1007/s40279-013-0090-5
sources.telemanas2024: Press Information Bureau, Government of India. Tele MANAS: Revolutionizing Mental Health Care in India. October 2024. static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2024/oct/doc20241013415701.pdf

sources.bell2023: Bell L et al. Integrating deloading into strength and physique sports training programmes: an international Delphi consensus approach. Sports Med Open 2023;9:87. doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00633-0

blocks.text: Motivation is often discussed and rarely measured. One part has been studied: why some reasons for training last while others fade. Much of the rest is sensible practice without strong evidence, and this chapter labels it that way.
It also draws an important line between low motivation, which can be a training problem, and low mood, which is not.
Motivation is often set against discipline. Research on this has looked at something else: whether your reasons come from you, or feel pushed on you.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise. Valuing the outcome tended to predict starting more strongly, while enjoying or finding the activity itself worthwhile better predicted long-term exercise. {teixeira2012}
Feeling competent and having more intrinsic motives also predicted exercise across many groups. {teixeira2012}
Most of the studies were non-experimental, so this shows association, not proven cause. {teixeira2012}

blocks.text: So the question is not only whether you can summon willpower on a bad day. It is whether your reason for training tends to last through bad days.
Wanting to look different is a fair reason to start. The same review found mixed evidence for body-related motives as a predictor of exercise. {teixeira2012}

blocks.title: What to do with that
paras: Keep your physique goal. Add a second reason that does not depend on the mirror: getting stronger at something specific, enjoying your session, or improving a skill.

blocks.text: When low motivation is a training problem
Not wanting to train can sometimes be information about your plan. Before treating it as a character flaw, check these:

head: Check
Why
rows: Stress predicted less activity in most prospective studies. {stults2014}
More is not always better, and recovery has a cost.
Too little food can leave you flat.

blocks.text: Dread and flatness are not proven measures of training stress. Treat them as a prompt to check the list above. Your logged performance over weeks is a better guide.
When it is not a training problem

blocks.title: Signs that need a clinician, not a lighter week
paras: Low mood or loss of interest most of the day, most days, for two weeks or more, including things you normally enjoy.
Sleep or appetite changes that do not follow your training.
Training that feels compulsive: distress at missing a session, training through injury or illness, or sessions pushing out work, study or relationships.
Food rules narrowing, or guilt and compensation after eating.
Constant worry about not being muscular enough, whatever your mirror or log shows.
Using alcohol or other substances to manage how you feel.
Thoughts of harming yourself. In India, call Tele-MANAS on 14416 at any time, or your local emergency services. {telemanas2024}
None of this means you failed at discipline. These are reasons to talk to a qualified clinician, and a handbook cannot assess you.

blocks.text: Exercise may help your mood, and trials suggest it can ease depression. {noetel2024} That is not a reason to manage these signs alone.

A lighter week when training feels heavy is reasonable and common. The guidance comes from expert agreement, not experiments. {bell2023} So it is a fair choice, not a requirement. Sometimes the honest reason is that you would rather train next month than grind through this one.
These cost nothing and many people like them. Take what helps and ignore the rest.

head: Practice
Status
rows: Comparing yourself with your past self, not others
Untested as a method here, but it fits the finding on competence. {teixeira2012}
Untested here. Your log does this for you.
Untested here for training. Pleasant and harmless.
No claim made here. If comparison feeds worry about your body, see the warning above.
Goals about actions, not just outcomes

items: **Treating low motivation as a moral failure.** Sleep, stress, volume or food may explain it.
**Waiting to feel motivated before starting.** Start small instead.
**Relying only on appearance.** Add a second reason.
**Taking a lighter week for something that is not a training problem.**
**Assuming untested means useless.** It means untested.
Reasons that come from you are linked with continuing to train.
Valuing results helps you start. Finding training worthwhile is more linked with continuing.
Appearance is a mixed predictor. Keep the goal and add a second reason.
Check sleep, stress, volume and food before blaming yourself.
Lasting low mood, compulsive training and thoughts of self-harm need qualified support.

title: Building habits that last
summary: How long it takes, and what actually helps.

sources.smith2024: Smith AE et al. Time to form a habit: a systematic review and meta-analysis of health behaviour habit formation and its determinants. Healthcare 2024;12(23):2488. doi:10.3390/healthcare12232488
sources.ma2023: Ma H et al. Effects of habit formation interventions on physical activity habit strength: meta-analysis and meta-regression. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 2023;20:109. doi:10.1186/s12966-023-01493-3

blocks.text: Habit formation has been measured, and the findings are less tidy than the popular version and more useful. It takes longer than you may have heard, people differ enormously, and missing a day matters less than the all-or-nothing story claims.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, with results that vary a lot
paras: A review of 20 studies with 2,601 people looked at health habits. Four studies reported timing: median times of 59 to 66 days, mean times of 106 to 154 days, and individuals ranging from 4 to 335 days. {smith2024}
Habit scores improved overall (effect size 0.69, 0.49 to 0.88): physical activity 0.69, diet 0.57, flossing 1.11. {smith2024}
Most studies had a high risk of bias, and the authors note the number of studies was small. {smith2024}

blocks.text: You may have heard "21 days". These results point to much longer. Two months of deliberate repetition before training feels automatic is a normal result. It does not mean you are bad at this.
These findings come from the same review, on a thin base.

head: Factor
Finding
rows: Morning practice generally gave stronger habits. {smith2024}
Self-selected habits generally gave stronger habits. {smith2024}

blocks.title: Pick your own habit
paras: Choose the habit you would actually keep. Attach it to something already steady in your day, and do it in the morning if that works for you. Give it a couple of months before adding another.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, with a small effect
paras: Ten studies found habit formation programmes increased physical activity habit strength (effect size 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48). Problem solving was linked with better results (0.36, 0.17 to 0.55). Social reward was linked with worse results after adjustment, based on only two studies. {ma2023}

blocks.text: Deliberate habit work helps, by a modest amount. Be sceptical of anyone promising a system that transforms your consistency.
Problem solving is simple: work out what usually stops you, and decide in advance what you will do when it happens.
Missing a day is not a relapse
In one well-known study, missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation. {lally2010} One missed session is a missed session. Most of the damage comes from what you decide next.

head: What happened
Reasonable response
rows: Train at your next planned time. Nothing else changes.
Ate a meal outside your plan
Missed a week for exams, work or illness
Return at a manageable load. Do not try to make up the sessions.
Treat it as a restart, not a failure.

blocks.text: "Never miss twice" is a catchy saying, not a finding.
This is a menu, not a schedule, since self-selected habits did better. {smith2024} The order is not based on a direct comparison.

head: Habit
Why it earns a place
rows: Aim for 7 or more hours, regularly. {aasm2015}
It has a clear number. See [[protein|Protein]].
Eating in a way you could keep up for a year
Long-term success depends on sticking with it. {aragon2017}
Simple, easy to cue and a reasonable first habit.

blocks.text: Self-monitoring was among the methods used in these programmes, though its own effect could not be isolated. {ma2023} A checklist is reasonable, but unproven by itself. Track a few things you chose, and review them weekly. Your Levlofit habit list is enough for this.

items: **Expecting automatic behaviour in three weeks.** It often takes about two months or longer.
**Following someone else's habit plan.** Self-selected habits did better.
**Starting several habits at once.** You may conclude you lack discipline when none stick.
**Treating one missed day as failure.**
**Expecting habits to replace training, sleep and protein.** They support those things.
**Judging a training habit by how it feels.** Look at your attendance over weeks.
Median time to form a habit was about 59 to 66 days, with individuals from 4 to 335 days.
Habit programmes work, by a modest amount.
Choose your own habit, attach it to a steady cue, and give it about two months.
Plan for what usually stops you.
One missed session does not undo the process.

title: Daily steps
summary: How many steps actually matter, and why 10,000 is not a magic number.

sources.paluch2022: Paluch AE et al. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health 2022;7(3):e219-e228.

blocks.text: Walking more is one of the simplest health wins, and you do not need 10,000 steps to get most of it.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: More daily steps went with lower risk, and the benefit levelled off at a lower count for older adults. Risk of death was 40 to 53% lower in the most active step groups compared with the least. {paluch2022}

items: **Walk after meals.** Ten minutes after lunch and dinner adds up fast.
**Take calls standing.** Pace while you talk.
**Use the stairs.** Skip the lift for a few floors.
Walking more is one of the simplest health wins.
The benefit levels off around 8,000 to 10,000 steps under 60, and 6,000 to 8,000 from 60.
Walk after meals, take calls standing and use the stairs.

blocks.text: The Nutrition volume covered how energy balance works. This chapter is about running a deficit for months: what protects your muscle, how far to trust a body-fat reading, and when getting leaner stops being a physique project and becomes a health problem.

About 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week is a reasonable pace, at the lower end as you get leaner. {helms2014} Slower loss can better preserve lean mass in leaner people, while a larger deficit may suit those with more body fat. {aragon2017}
What protects muscle in a deficit

head: What to do
What the ISSN says
rows: Resistance training has shown an impressive ability to preserve muscle during very low-calorie dieting, at least in untrained or obese people. {aragon2017}
2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of **fat-free** mass may be required in lean, resistance-trained people eating below their needs. {aragon2017}

blocks.text: Extra cardio, fat burners and meal timing are smaller than these two.

blocks.title: What decides the outcome
paras: The ISSN states that the long-term success of a diet depends on sticking with it. {aragon2017} A diet you finish beats a stricter one you drop in week six.

blocks.text: You cannot choose where it comes off

Training one body part is a poor way to lose the fat over it. Expect that fat to change as your overall body fat changes. Later chapters in this volume are about building what is underneath, which is a separate job.
Body-fat percentage is a weaker number than it looks

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, from one study
paras: Three body-fat scanners using electrical impedance were compared with a DEXA scan in 93 people. Agreement was unacceptable for a consumer scale (0.61), poor for a gym analyser (0.88) and moderate for a medical analyser (0.91). {merrigan2022}
When 36 people retested after 12 weeks, the subtle changes in body fat did not agree between these devices and DEXA. {merrigan2022}
All three repeated well within a session. Consistent is not the same as accurate. {merrigan2022}

blocks.text: So treat a body-fat reading as a wide band, not an exact figure. A scale reading of 17.4% is false precision. Your waist measurement, seven-day average weight, training log and photos are more practical. The body-fat tool in Levlofit gives an estimate too, so read it the same way.

paras: The International Olympic Committee describes Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport as a syndrome of harmful health and performance outcomes in female and male athletes exposed to low energy availability, meaning too little food for the exercise they do. {mountjoy2023}
That statement is about athletes, so it is used here for its warning signs, not for numbers about you.

You get a bone stress injury.
Sex drive, mood, sleep or tolerance of cold fall together over weeks of dieting.

Your strength keeps falling even though you are training as planned.
Food rules keep narrowing, eating brings guilt or compensation, or the scale decides how your day goes.
You cannot stop cutting, even after reaching your target.
None of this is a failure of discipline. See a doctor, and where eating is involved, someone who works with disordered eating.

blocks.title: Read this first
paras: Most of this chapter is not science. "Aesthetic" is a judgement. No study shows one set of proportions is correct, and nothing ranks shoulders above calves. You are entitled to disagree with all of it. What is evidence-based here is narrow: muscle grows with loaded work, you cannot choose where fat comes off, and some popular rules do not hold up.

blocks.text: The usual ideal is three things: enough muscle to see, body fat low enough to show it, and muscle spread in a way many people call balanced.

head: Quality
Status
rows: Trainable, with a floor. See [[body-fat-lean|Body fat and getting lean]].
A cultural preference, not a measurement.
A preference. Small differences are normal. Marked or painful ones are for a clinician.

head: Reason
Status

Well supported. Growth rises with sets for that muscle. {pelland2025}
Strength training lowers sports injury risk
Most people prefer how it looks

blocks.text: It is **not established** that neglecting a muscle group causes injury, so that is not one of the reasons here.
Two training rules that do not hold up

blocks.title: "Slow reps build more muscle": moderate evidence against
paras: A review of eight studies found muscle growth was similar with repetitions lasting from 0.5 to 8 seconds. Very slow repetitions of over 10 seconds looked worse, though few controlled studies make this hard to settle. All the included studies took sets to failure. {schoenfeld2015}

blocks.text: So slowing every repetition is not a growth strategy. Control still matters, so you reach your full range and keep the work on the target muscle. Tempo itself is not the driver.

"Good technique prevents injury" also goes beyond the evidence here. Technique is a sensible default. A better-supported reason for a full range is that loaded, full-range training improves range of motion. {alizadeh2023}
What each muscle is said to add
This whole table is convention, not measurement. It would change with the viewer, the era and the clothes.

head: Muscle
Usually credited with
rows: Fullness. This is a claim about one part of a muscle, which has thin support.

blocks.text: Training for one part of a muscle

blocks.title: Thin evidence
paras: Claims that an exercise builds the upper chest or outer thigh rest on very little. In this Handbook, the direct evidence is one trial in 30 people, on the lower body only. {burke2025}
Varying your exercises and angles is reasonable, low-cost and possibly useful. Building a whole plan around sculpting one region claims something nobody has shown.

blocks.text: When physique focus becomes a problem

blocks.title: Evidence: emerging, from a small literature
paras: Muscle dysmorphia is a body image disorder with an obsessive preoccupation with muscularity, along with behaviours such as excessive exercise, rigid dieting and frequent body checking. A review of ten studies found symptoms moderately linked with obsessive-compulsive traits (r about 0.24), and higher among steroid users than non-users (d about 0.45). {cinaroglu2025}

blocks.text: The V-taper is the contrast between your shoulder and upper-back width and your waist. It is a popular goal, often sold with claims that do not hold up.
Wanting one is an aesthetic preference, not a health or performance target. This chapter is about what is achievable, not whether it is worth achieving.
Three contributors, two of them trainable

head: Contributor
Trainable?
Status
rows: Skeleton: shoulder and hip width, rib cage
Bone width does not widen with training once you have finished growing.
Muscle over the frame: shoulders, lats, upper back
Body fat, especially at the waist
You cannot train your waist lean.

blocks.text: So two people with the same plan and effort can end up with different tapers. Much of that difference is likely to be skeletal, and it is no failure of motivation.
What drives growth in your shoulders and lats is the same as anywhere else: enough weekly work directed at the muscle, progressed over time, with diminishing returns as sets rise. {pelland2025}

The claim that one exercise builds one part of a muscle has thin support. The direct evidence here is one lower-body study. {burke2025} Doing exercises that load a muscle in different positions is sensible and possibly useful. None of these is required.

head: Claim
Position
rows: "Heavy core and oblique work thickens your waist, so avoid it."
Not established. This is a belief, and no reason to skip trunk work.
"Train your abs to lose the fat over them."
Do not rely on it. Overall fat loss is what changes this.

blocks.text: What really changes how your waist looks is your overall body fat, which is neither quick nor selective.

blocks.title: Measure your waist, not a ratio
paras: Use a tape at the same spot every few weeks. Shoulder-to-waist targets online, including the "golden ratio", have no validated basis, so this Handbook gives none.

blocks.text: How you stand changes how you look in a photo. That is a claim about appearance, not health. [[posture|Posture and movement]] looks at the health claims.

items: **Expecting training to widen your bones.** It adds muscle over them.
**Skipping trunk work to protect your waist.** That belief is not established.
**Building a plan around sculpting regions.** The evidence is thin.
**Training your abs to reveal them.** That comes from overall fat loss.
**Adding shoulder and back sets without cutting elsewhere.** It costs recovery.
**Chasing a published ratio.** There is no validated target.
Bone is fixed, muscle responds to training, and fat cannot be lost selectively.
Shoulders and lats grow on the same dose-response as anything else.
Vary your exercises sensibly, but do not plan around sculpting.
Your waist responds to overall fat loss.
Two people with the same effort will still look different.

blocks.text: Bringing up a weak muscle is a popular topic with little direct research. This chapter gives you the one lever with evidence, what it costs, and what the rest of the usual advice is worth.

head: Meaning
Status
rows: A muscle you have trained less, which is smaller or weaker as a result
Real, and you can address it. Your log can show this.
A muscle you would prefer to look different
A preference, often a comparison with a different skeleton.

blocks.text: Only the first responds to more training. Muscle shape and limb length are individual, and exercise choice will not rewrite them.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: Muscle growth rises with weekly sets for that muscle, with diminishing returns as sets rise. {pelland2025}

blocks.title: Extra sets are not free
paras: Recovery has a cost. Adding work without removing any is a recovery decision disguised as a physique decision.

In practice, make it a **trade**: raise sets for the target muscle and lower them somewhere you are happy to hold steady for a while. Because returns shrink at higher volumes, a well-trained muscle may lose little from giving up a few sets. That is reasoning, not a tested result.

head: Advice
Grade
Comment
rows: The ACSM found exercise order did not affect muscle growth. {acsm2026} It may still help you give that muscle your best effort.
The lever is established. {pelland2025} "Gradually" is practical advice.
Improve technique so the target "does the work"
Technique helps you reach your range and stay comfortable. No growth claim is made here.
Change the exercise to hit it differently
Variety is cheap and reasonable. It is not a precise tool. {burke2025}
It improves range of motion. {alizadeh2023} It is not a specific fix for weak muscles.
With volume equal, frequency did not affect growth. {acsm2026}

blocks.text: People who train can see themselves as smaller than they are, and that worry can become a medical problem. {cinaroglu2025} These tools are more reliable than your impression:

head: Method
Good for
rows: Showing a movement you have trained or progressed less. Often the most reliable sign.
Useful over months, not month to month.
"Which muscle tires first in a big lift"
Not validated as a sign of a weak muscle.

blocks.title: Left and right are a different question
paras: Small differences between sides are normal. It is not established that single-side work corrects them. Marked or painful differences need a clinician, not a special training block.

blocks.text: Longer than most specialisation plans claim. A muscle that is behind may be months or years of work behind, and returns shrink as you add sets. {pelland2025} A block lasting a few weeks may show up in your log and not yet in a photo. Judge it by your log.

items: **Add sets everywhere at once.** Trade instead.
**Stop training muscles that are ahead.** That is a slower route to balance.
**Change your plan every few weeks.** Novelty does not solve this.
**Treat your anatomy as a training problem.** Shape and limb length do not respond to exercise choice.
**Copy someone else's specialisation routine** without knowing their training history.
**Believing an exercise targets one region.** That has thin support.
**Treating "train it first" as a growth technique.**
**Ignoring the recovery cost of extra sets.**
**Judging a six-week block by photos.**
**Confusing a real training gap with a preference,** or with a preoccupation that needs help.
More weekly sets for the muscle is the one established lever, with shrinking returns.
Trade sets rather than only adding them.
Exercise order, cues and exercise choice are weak tools for this.
Your anatomy is not a lagging muscle.
Judge the block by your log. The mirror runs on a longer clock.

blocks.title: Read this first
paras: The familiar story says certain postures are "poor", weak backs and tight chests cause them, and exercises correct them. The evidence does not support that story as stated. Posture is associated with some outcomes, and has not been shown to cause them. Most of the practical advice stays. What changes is why: comfort, strength and appearance, not correction.

blocks.title: Evidence: no consensus on cause
paras: A review of 41 systematic reviews looked at spine posture, physical activity and low back pain. They reported both positive and null associations for spine posture, prolonged standing, sitting, bending and twisting, awkward postures and heavy physical work. {swain2020}

Its conclusion: "Despite the availability of many reviews, there is no consensus regarding causality of physical exposure to LBP. Association has been documented but does not provide a causal explanation for LBP." {swain2020}

blocks.text: This does not say posture never matters, and it is no recommendation to slouch. It says the confident story, where bad posture causes your pain and fixing it cures your pain, is not established.
Forward head posture and neck pain

blocks.title: Evidence: association in adults, not established as cause
paras: A review of 15 cross-sectional studies found adults with neck pain had more forward head posture than those without. In adolescents there was no significant difference. Age played an important role. {mahmoud2019}
All the studies were cross-sectional, which means they measured people at one point in time, so this design cannot show which came first.

blocks.text: The missing link in adolescents is interesting. If this posture simply caused neck pain, you might expect the link at all ages. It might instead reflect age, or people in pain holding themselves differently. That is reasoning, not a finding.

blocks.text: This chapter adds no new evidence. It closes the volume where this Handbook most often has to say "this is not science".

In brief: muscle and body fat are the two things you can train here, and you cannot control where fat comes off. Proportion, taper, symmetry and posture correction are convention, reasoning or association.

head: Claim
What this volume found
rows: "You can burn fat from one area."
Do not rely on it. Overall fat loss is what matters.
"This exercise builds the upper chest or outer thigh."
Growth was similar from 0.5 to 8 seconds per repetition. {schoenfeld2015}
Linked in adults, not in adolescents, and cause is not shown. {mahmoud2019}
Muscle over the frame grows. Adult bone width does not change with training.
"A body-fat scale tells you your body fat."
It gives an estimate, and it tracked 12-week change poorly against DEXA. {merrigan2022}
Sweat is mostly fluid loss. Fat loss comes from a calorie deficit. {aragon2017}
"Lifting will make you bulky by accident."
Muscle grows slowly, so this is unlikely.

head: Question
Answer
rows: How long does an aesthetic physique take?
Usually years. Your log will often show change before a photo does.
Should I cut or bulk first?
This is practice, not a trial result. A larger deficit may suit those with more body fat, and slower loss helps leaner people keep lean mass. {aragon2017}
Can I build muscle and lose fat at once?
Often, especially if you are new, returning or carrying more body fat. No reliable rate is established.
See [[supplements-guide|Supplements]]. Creatine is the main one with strong support. {issncreatine}
How often should I change my plan?
Less often than most people do. Periodised plans were not found better for growth. {acsm2026}
Genes influence your frame and how you respond. Training decides what you do with them. That is a reason to stop comparing, not to stop training.

blocks.text: Tracking does not build muscle or remove fat. It reduces the error in your own judgement about whether something changed. The tools you use have errors of their own, and much of this volume is about handling them.
"You cannot improve what you never measure" is a management slogan. The closest evidence here suggests something more careful.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A review of randomised trials looked at self-weighing for weight loss. Only one study tested self-weighing alone, and there was no evidence it worked (-0.5 kg, -1.3 to 0.3). {madigan2015}
Adding self-weighing to a behaviour programme helped (-1.7 kg, -2.6 to -0.8). Programmes that included it beat minimal support (-3.4 kg, -4.2 to -2.6). {madigan2015}

blocks.text: So tracking does not do the work. It helps you steer the training and eating you are already doing.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, from one small study
paras: In 41 mothers of young children, self-measured waist, hip and neck measurements were compared with a trained technician's. Agreement was high (0.97, 0.96 and 0.84). blocks.text: So self-measuring can work well with simple instruction. But 10% of a 90 cm waist is 9 cm, far more than you would expect to change in a month. And this was a small group of women, so it may not fit everyone.

blocks.text: Body weight is the cheapest measurement in this Handbook, and among the most misread. A decent scale has little error, while your body's daily changes are large. That combination decides everything below.

blocks.title: Use a seven-day average
paras: Judge your weight by a seven-day average, not one reading. Weigh most days in the same conditions, average the last seven readings, and compare that average week to week.

blocks.text: Averaging works because daily swings partly cancel out. Your body does not change when you take an average. Your measurement improves.
A rolling average also updates every day, so one missed weigh-in does little harm.

blocks.text: What you want to measure moves over weeks. Other parts move within a day, sometimes by more than a real week's change.

blocks.text: Goal setting is taught with great confidence and studied much less. This chapter says which advice has evidence behind it.
SMART goals are a drafting aid

SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. No evidence reviewed here shows that writing a training goal this way changes your results. It is a useful checklist for writing clearly, nothing more. Being measurable and achievable do matter, because this volume can tell you what you can measure and how fast change can happen.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: In ten studies of habit programmes for physical activity, problem solving was linked with better results (0.36, 0.17 to 0.55), and action planning was among the common techniques. The overall effect was small to medium (0.31, 0.14 to 0.48). {ma2023}

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, from two more sources
paras: **Whose goal it is matters.** A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise. {teixeira2012}
**Choosing your own helps.** In a review of 20 studies, self-selected habits generally gave stronger habits. {smith2024}

blocks.title: What this recommends

blocks.text: Many people stop training. What distinguishes those who do not? The evidence has a partial answer, and it does not come down to willpower.

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise. Valuing the outcome tended to predict starting, while intrinsic motivation better predicted long-term exercise. Feeling competent also predicted exercise. Most studies were non-experimental, so this shows association, not proven cause. {teixeira2012}

blocks.text: In practice, the reason that gets you started may not be the one that keeps you going. It helps if training becomes something you would do anyway.
How long before it takes less effort
Median time to form a habit was 59 to 66 days, and individuals ranged from 4 to 335 days. {smith2024} Someone at the far end took most of a year and was not doing anything wrong.

Stress predicted less physical activity in 76.4% of 55 prospective studies. Some found the opposite, with habitually active people exercising more under stress. {stults2014} So the years you have already put in may help protect you.

Missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation in one well-known study. {lally2010} "Never miss twice" is a catchy saying, not a finding. Keep it if it helps, but do not treat a second miss as failure.
When a month is hard, choose between your full plan and a smaller one, not your full plan and nothing. These are practical suggestions.

title: Baseline tests
summary: Six simple tests, and what they can and cannot tell you.

blocks.text: Moving up in any discipline should mean showing a real ability, not just finishing a number of weeks. These six simple field tests give you an honest starting point. They need little more than a bar and a stopwatch, and all are optional.
Levlofit's own level checks are set per goal in the app. The tests here are for tracking yourself, and they do not set your level there.
What a field test can tell you

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate, with an important limit
paras: One study of field tests including pull-ups and push-ups found they were not valid measures of absolute strength, but were valid for strength relative to body weight. The study was in 94 children aged 9 to 10, so it applies to adults only by reasoning. {pate1993}

blocks.text: In practice, a push-up or pull-up count is a repeatable way to compare yourself with yourself over months. Do not treat it as a stand-in for a one-repetition maximum.
Warm up first, and stop when your form breaks. These are practical test descriptions.

items: **Strict push-ups.** Full range, chest near the floor, no sagging hips, until form breaks.
**Strict pull-ups or chin-ups.** Start from a dead hang, chin clears the bar, no swinging.
**Dead hang.** Time how long your grip holds.
**Plank or hollow-body hold.** Time until the position collapses.
**1 km run.** Flat ground, at your own pace, timed.
**Standing broad jump.** Take off and land on two feet. Measure to your heels. Take your best of three.

blocks.title: These are maximal efforts
paras: If you have a joint, tendon or heart condition that a hard test could aggravate, skip that test and ask your doctor first. Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness. A partial baseline is still useful.

blocks.text: Retest every 8 to 12 weeks if you want a check, at the start of a new block rather than at the end of a tiring one. This interval is practical guidance. A result that has not moved is information, not failure. Change one thing at a time.

items: These tests measure how well you move your own body.
They are good for comparing yourself over time, and poor stand-ins for maximum strength.
The main study behind this was in children, so treat its findings as a guide.

blocks.text: Strength is a skill as well as muscle. Lift heavy, practise the same lifts often, and rest long enough to lift well.
Heavy loads build more maximal strength than light loads. {schoenfeld2017l}

blocks.text: In practice, rest long enough that your next heavy set is a good one. That is often 2 minutes or more on the big lifts.

title: Combining different kinds of training
summary: How strength and cardio fit together.

sources.schumann2022: Schumann M et al. Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training for skeletal muscle size and function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2022;52(3):601-612. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01587-7

blocks.text: Few people train only one thing forever. A runner may want strength, and a lifter may want better fitness. The old fear was that mixing strength and cardio would blunt the results of both. The current evidence is more specific, and kinder.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: A review of 43 studies compared combined aerobic and strength training with strength training alone. It found no meaningful loss in maximal strength (effect size -0.06, -0.20 to 0.09) or muscle growth (-0.01, -0.16 to 0.18). {schumann2022}
The gain that did suffer was explosive strength (-0.28, -0.48 to -0.08), more so when both were done in the same session than when sessions were at least 3 hours apart. {schumann2022}

blocks.text: So strength and muscle gains generally hold up. If explosive work matters to you, keep it apart from cardio when you can.

This is practical guidance. Choose one main goal, and let it have first claim on your training days. Add other kinds of training at a smaller, steady dose. If you run out of days, trim the smaller dose first. Levlofit lets you rank your goals, and your plan shows you how they fit your week.
Skill and speed work is best done while you are fresh. In practice:

items: Put jumps, sprints and new skills early in a session.
Place them before your most tiring session of the week when you can.
Do not stack them straight after a hard session on the same day.

blocks.text: You do not need a separate lighter-week schedule for each kind of training. Reduce your whole week together. Hard interval or station sessions count as fatigue too, even though they are not lifting. See [[deload-week|Deload week]].

Whatever your goal, WHO recommends all adults do 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix, along with regular muscle-strengthening activity. {who2020}

blocks.text: In running, the hardest session is not always the most important one. A running week can be built mostly from comfortable running, with faster work added in small amounts once that base is secure.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong, for health
paras: WHO recommends adults do 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix. {who2020}

blocks.text: A week of only hard running is hard to sustain at that volume. A week of mostly easy running is much easier to keep up.

blocks.title: Evidence: uncertain, from one exploratory study
paras: A one-year study followed 874 novice runners. Overall, injury rates did not differ significantly between those increasing weekly distance by under 10%, 10 to 30%, or over 30%. {nielsen2014}

For distance-related injuries specifically, those increasing by more than 30% had a higher rate than those under 10% (hazard ratio 1.59), but the interval included no effect (0.96 to 2.66). The authors suggest novices may be well advised to stay under 30% a week. {nielsen2014}

blocks.text: So no percentage is proven safe, including the popular "10% rule". A sensible approach is to change one thing at a time: distance, number of sessions or intensity. Pain that continues or gets worse is a reason to stop and get it checked.

blocks.title: Stop when quality drops
paras: If a hard session has fallen well below your intended pace, you are training a slower pace while tired. End it early. Stop right away if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.

blocks.text: Athletic training here means power: moving your own body quickly and forcefully. It is usually trained early in a session, before anything that would tire you.

paras: A meta-analysis of 56 studies on jump training found the largest gains in jump height came from programmes longer than 10 weeks, with more than 20 sessions, and with more than 50 jumps a session. Combining jump types beat using only one. Adding weight gave no extra benefit. {saez2009}

blocks.text: This order is practical reasoning. Learn to control a landing before you try to jump higher. Learn to jump before you ask your legs to do the same at speed. Then build acceleration, slowing down and changing direction.

paras: Top-speed sprinting and advanced jumps, such as depth jumps and high-volume single-leg bounding, have real technical demands. A qualified coach who can watch you in person will catch problems sooner. Build up slowly, and stop if you feel pain in a joint or tendon.

title: HYROX
summary: Eight runs and eight stations, always in the same order.

blocks.text: HYROX is a race with a fixed format: 1 km of running followed by one functional workout station, repeated eight times. {hyrox} Because the format is fixed, you can train for exactly what race day will ask.

blocks.title: Check the current rules
paras: Weights, distances and format details are set by HYROX and can change. Check the current official rules before a race. {hyrox}

blocks.text: The eight stations, in race order
A 1 km run comes before every station. {hyrox}
This is practical guidance. Practise the same eight movements in the same order, in circuits you can scale. Start with fewer rounds and add more as you improve.

If you lack equipment, use the closest substitute and be clear with yourself that it is not the real station. A bike or rower can stand in for a SkiErg, and a bodyweight walking lunge can stand in for sandbag lunges.

items: **Pace your runs as well as your stations.** A common mistake is treating the runs as recovery. Both cost you time on the clock.
**Choose a pace you can hold for all eight runs,** not just the first three.
**Build up in stages.** Start with one station and its run, then half the format, then all eight, moving on when the shorter version feels comfortable.

blocks.text: Combined training generally does not hurt strength or muscle gains. {schumann2022} See [[combining-training|Combining different kinds of training]].

title: Boxing: solo training
summary: Everything here can be trained alone. Sparring cannot.

sources.schumann2022: Schumann M et al. Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training for skeletal muscle size and function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2022;52(3):601-612. doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01587-7

blocks.text: Boxing is two activities with one name. One is solo technique and conditioning: footwork, shadowboxing, bag work and skipping. The other is partner work, including sparring. This chapter covers only the first. This whole chapter is practical guidance.

blocks.title: Sparring and partner drills need a coach
paras: Do not spar from a handbook or an app. A qualified coach in the room can watch your guard, correct your distance and stop a session the moment it becomes unsafe. Levlofit cannot do that. Find a registered club and coach for any partner work, and get medical attention after any head injury.

head: Movement
What it trains
rows: The same combinations against real resistance, at a set pace
Quick, precise steps without crossing your feet

blocks.text: A classic format is rounds: three minutes of work and one minute of rest. Start with about three rounds and build up slowly. If your session is short, do fewer rounds instead of cutting a drill out of the rotation.
On the heavy bag, wrap your hands and wear gloves, and build up how hard you hit. Stop if your wrists, knuckles or shoulders hurt.
Keep some strength training in your week, with about two sessions, and fill the rest with solo rounds. Combined training generally does not hurt strength or muscle gains. {schumann2022}

title: Home and bodyweight training
summary: What you have decides what you do.

blocks.text: Much fitness content assumes a full gym and treats everything else as a compromise. Levlofit asks what you actually have, and builds your plan around that. This chapter explains the thinking, so you can make good swaps yourself.

The ACSM concludes that many forms of resistance training work, and calls for programmes to be fitted to the person. {acsm2026} A well-run bodyweight plan and a well-run barbell plan are both real training. A poor substitution, made without knowing it, is the real problem.

head: You have
What it opens up
rows: Dumbbell and carry movements, plus bodyweight

blocks.text: Some movements need somewhere to hang or stand. A pull-up needs a bar, and a box jump needs a box. A doorway pull-up bar is one of the cheapest items that can open up a lot of pulling work. Fit it securely, follow its limits and test it before you trust your weight to it.

If a movement needs equipment you lack, use the swap test from [[push-sessions|Building a push session]]: same movement pattern, same joint action. If nothing matches, choose the closest option and be honest with yourself that it is a different exercise. You can tell Levlofit what you have, and ask it to swap an exercise.

title: Training as a woman
summary: Lifting, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and after birth: what the evidence says.

blocks.text: Women build muscle much as men do: across studies, muscle grew by a similar percentage in women and men. {refalo2025}

head: Myth
Evidence
rows: You must train differently in each cycle phase
Cycle effects on performance are small and individual
Exercise is safe and helpful in most pregnancies

blocks.title: Evidence: moderate
paras: A meta-analysis of 78 studies found performance may be slightly lower in the early follicular phase, but effects were trivial and varied, so general phase-based rules are not supported. {mcnulty2020}

items: **Track.** Keep your own note of energy and mood, if that helps.
**Adjust.** On low days lower the load a little; on good days push.
**Keep going.** No phase needs you to stop training.

blocks.text: The Canadian guideline points to 150 minutes a week of moderate activity during a healthy pregnancy. {mottola2018}

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: WHO advises pregnant and postpartum women without contraindications to stay active throughout pregnancy and after birth, with at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week and a mix of aerobic and muscle-strengthening work. Women who were active before pregnancy can usually continue. {who2020}

title: Training after 40
summary: Why strength and balance matter more with age, and how to train safely.

blocks.text: Muscle and balance fade with age unless you train them. It is never too late: older adults gain strength well.

blocks.title: Evidence: strong
paras: WHO advises older adults to do varied balance and strength work on 3 or more days a week to prevent falls. {who2020}

blocks.text: Older adults need more training than younger adults to keep muscle size. {bickel2011}

items: **Longer warm-up.** 10 minutes, gradually heavier.
**Moderate reps.** 8 to 15 reps with good control.
**Balance every week.** Single-leg stands, step-ups, heel-to-toe walking.
**Recover.** Levlofit rule: 48 hours between hard sessions for the same muscles.

paras: Levlofit builds plans for ages 18 to 80. Over 65, or living with a long-term condition? Read [[safety-first|Safe to start]] again and check with your doctor before hard training.

title: Building a week, and troubleshooting
summary: The whole book put together in one week.

sources.who2020: Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med 2020;54:1451-1462.

blocks.text: This closing chapter walks through how to put training into a week, then answers some common questions. It is practical guidance built on the rest of this Handbook. Your Levlofit plan does this for you, and this chapter helps you understand and adjust it.

items: **Start with your main goal.** It has first claim on your days.
**Add other goals at a smaller, steady dose.** See [[combining-training|Combining different kinds of training]].
**Fit it to your equipment.** Use what you actually have.
**Respect your limits.** Remove anything that aggravates a known problem. If your session is short, trim small exercises first.
**Set your starting point honestly.** Start from where you actually are.

blocks.text: For health, aim for WHO's guidelines as well: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix, along with muscle strengthening. {who2020}

No one calendar suits everyone. A useful pattern is to build the basics before specialising, check your progress at the end of each block, and reduce your training when fatigue says so. A year of training is that cycle repeated. Your goals and equipment can change between cycles.

head: Question
Answer
rows: My extra goal has no room this week.
You may not have enough days for both. Keep your main goal, trim the extra one, or add a day if you can recover from it.
My skill is stuck on one step.
Skills move up when you can do the next step with control, not because time has passed. Practise, and retest.
My plan has a different exercise from what I expected.
You may not have the equipment, or a limit you told Levlofit about may rule it out. Check your equipment and limits, or ask for a swap.
Can I add sparring or partner drills?
Do this only with a qualified coach in person. See [[boxing-solo|Boxing: solo training]].
Choose fewer days you can actually keep. Stress and busy periods often show up as missed sessions. {stults2014}
Reduce your training, and check sleep and food. See [[plateaus|Breaking through plateaus]].

items: Start from your main goal, your days and your equipment.
Build the basics before specialising.
Review at the end of each block, and reduce when fatigue says so.
